etymology: Derived from краса ("beauty"), from an old root meaning "beautiful".
commonMistakes: The short forms красив/красива/красиво are used in predicate position (Она красива), while the long form tends to modify a noun.

etymology: A lexicalized neuter short form of важный ("important"), used as an impersonal predicate.
commonMistakes: Distinguish the adjective use of важный from the impersonal predicate use of важно ("it is important that...").

aspectUsage: Imperfective for habitual/repeated "going out"; use the perfective выйти for a single completed exit.
etymology: Prefix вы- ("out") plus ходить ("to walk") — "to walk outward".
commonMistakes: выходить замуж is specifically used for a woman "getting married"; for a man, use жениться.

example.ru: Она выходит из дома в семь.
example.gloss: She leaves the house at seven.

examples.gloss: He's going out for a break.
The magazine comes out once a month.
The book was published last year.

synonymComparison.note: a close synonym: выходить focuses on exiting (inside to outside), while уходить means leaving a place altogether.

past.f.gloss: She used to go out on stage.

past.n.gloss: Everything used to turn out differently.

past.pl.ru: Мы выходили на прогулку каждый день.
past.pl.gloss: We used to go for a walk every day.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'm going out in five minutes.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Are you getting off at the next stop?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He's dropping out of the game.

nonpast.1pl.ru: Мы выходим на рынок в этом году.
nonpast.1pl.gloss: We're entering the market this year.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Are you getting off here?

imperative.pl.gloss: Come out one at a time.

etymology: Derived from начать ("to begin"); the original sense is "the beginning".
commonMistakes: в начале ("at the beginning [of a period]") and с начала ("from the start [over]") have different meanings.

etymology: From Old Church Slavonic пальць, originally referring specifically to the thumb, now used for any finger.
commonMistakes: Note the fleeting vowel that drops in declension (палец→пальца).

etymology: From an old oblique form of край ("edge"); the sense shifted from "outside the edge" to "excluding".
commonMistakes: кроме requires the genitive case (кроме меня, not кроме мне).

etymology: Derived from сила ("strength"); some trace the root to a Proto-Indo-European sense of "binding".
commonMistakes: The adverb form сильно is also used colloquially to mean "very" as an intensifier.

etymology: Derived from здоровый ("healthy"), but colloquially fixed as an exclamation meaning "great/awesome".
commonMistakes: Distinguish the original "in a healthy way" sense from the colloquial exclamatory "great!" sense, by context.

etymology: A fossilized form of в + перед ("front"); it means "forward".
commonMistakes: Distinguish directional вперёд ("forward", motion) from locational впереди ("in front", static position).

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "coming to want something"; use the imperfective хотеть for an ongoing state of wanting.
etymology: Prefix за- ("onset") plus хотеть ("to want") — "to begin wanting".
commonMistakes: Shares the same irregular stem alternation as хотеть (singular захоч-, plural захот-).

governance.pattern: accusative or infinitive (what one comes to want)

examples.gloss: She suddenly wanted to go home.

synonymComparison.note: захотеть (the subject actively wants) contrasts with the impersonal захотелось (dative + 'felt like doing'), which is less willful.

past.f.gloss: She came to want the truth.

past.n.gloss: There was a sudden urge to change everything.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You'll want to come back.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to breathe"; related to дышать (to breathe).
commonMistakes: Contrasted with тело ("body"), душа refers to the spiritual/inner self — keep that contrast in mind.

etymology: Derived from внимать ("to heed", archaic); the original sense was "directing the mind toward something".
commonMistakes: Use обратить внимание на + accusative (not "обратить внимание о").

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing the ongoing process of studying. научиться is its perfective partner, meaning "to master/learn [a skill]".
etymology: The reflexive form of учить ("to teach") — "to make oneself learn".
commonMistakes: Don't confuse учить (transitive, "to teach / memorize") with учиться (intransitive, "to study").

examples.gloss: He learned to swim as a child.

synonymComparison.note: учиться (to study as a student) and заниматься (to work on/study independently) overlap, but учиться specifically refers to being enrolled in studies.

past.n.gloss: Everything was easy to learn as a child.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'm studying to become an engineer.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Are you doing a graduate degree?

etymology: A slang term of unclear origin, possibly from Romani; a youth-register word.
commonMistakes: A very casual slang term — avoid it with superiors or in formal settings.

etymology: Borrowed from French compagnie, ultimately from Latin companio ("one who shares bread").
commonMistakes: It carries both the "company (business)" and "group of friends" senses — context decides which.

etymology: Derived from чувствовать ("to feel").
commonMistakes: без чувств is an idiom meaning "unconscious" — don't read it literally.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to chase/hunt".
commonMistakes: Note the figurative use in expressions like холодная война ("cold war").

etymology: Derived from считать ("to count"); the original sense was "a count/tally".
commonMistakes: It covers both "bank account" and "restaurant bill" — context decides which.

etymology: The adverbial form of давний ("long-past"), lexicalized.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse давно ("for a long time / long ago") with недавно ("recently").

etymology: A compound of сам ("self") and летать ("to fly") — "that which flies by itself".
commonMistakes: "By plane" is на самолёте (prepositional case).

etymology: From Old Church Slavonic жрьтва, originally a religious "offering", which developed into "sacrifice/victim".
commonMistakes: жертва is grammatically feminine but can refer to a male victim too — a mismatch between grammatical and real-world gender.

etymology: An agent noun derived from убить ("to kill").
commonMistakes: убийца declines like a feminine -а noun grammatically, but modifiers and verbs agree with the real gender of the person (common-gender noun).

aspectUsage: A stative verb (location) with no perfective counterpart.
etymology: A reflexive derivative of найти ("to find") — "to find oneself [somewhere] → to be located".
commonMistakes: находиться means purely "to be located" — don't confuse it with найти/находить ("to find").

synonymComparison.note: находиться ('to be located,' more formal) is close to быть ('to be,' general), but находиться is used specifically to state location.

past.m.gloss: The house was located far away.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: The building is located near the metro.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You're in the risk zone.

etymology: Derived from болеть ("to be sick").
commonMistakes: The nominalized use больной ("a patient") is also common — distinguish it from the adjective use.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "bringing [a person]"; use the imperfective приводить for repeated/habitual bringing.
etymology: Prefix при- ("arrival") plus вести ("to lead") — "to lead to arrival".
commonMistakes: Don't confuse привести (bringing a person, on foot) with принести (bringing an object, carried).

example.gloss: He brought a friend to the party.

examples.gloss: She brought the children to school.
He gives an example every time.
This road leads to the center.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: привести is for bringing a person (leading them), while принести is for bringing an object (carrying it).

past.n.gloss: The decision led to a dispute.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll lead the team to victory.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you bring the client tomorrow?

etymology: A compound of так ("so") and же (emphatic particle).
commonMistakes: Nearly synonymous with тоже, but также is more literary/formal.

etymology: Borrowed from the English name John.
commonMistakes: As a foreign name it still declines regularly (genitive Джона etc.).

etymology: A fossilized instrumental form of вечер ("evening"), now used as an adverb.
commonMistakes: The instrumental of the noun вечер and the adverb "in the evening" look identical — be aware of the different function.

etymology: From an old prefix оп- plus an archaic root meaning "to take" — "to take again → again".
commonMistakes: Nearly synonymous with снова, but опять is more colloquial and can carry a note of irritation.

etymology: A compound of вообще ("in general") and the emphatic particle -то, lexicalized into a colloquial discourse marker.
commonMistakes: A colloquial way to soften a correction or introduce a caveat — inappropriate in formal registers.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "coming to like something"; use the imperfective нравиться for an ongoing state of liking.
etymology: Prefix по- plus нравиться ("to please").
commonMistakes: Takes the same dative construction as нравиться (мне понравилось = "I liked it").

governance.pattern: dative (person who liked it) + nominative (thing liked)

synonymComparison.note: понравиться ('to like, a one-time impression') differs in depth from полюбить ('to come to love,' a deeper, lasting shift in feeling).

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll win them over right away.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Your colleagues will like you.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of "conversing"; use поговорить for a single completed conversation.
etymology: Prefix раз- plus говорить ("to speak") — "to speak back and forth".
commonMistakes: Unlike говорить (to speak in general), разговаривать emphasizes the two-way dialogue.

examples.ru: Мы разговариваем по телефону каждый день.
examples.gloss: We talk on the phone every day.

synonymComparison.note: разговаривать ('to converse,' focused on the exchange) is close to говорить ('to speak,' more general) but differs in nuance.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Do you talk in your sleep?

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you speak Russian?

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "drinking [something] up"; use выпивать for repeated/ongoing drinking.
etymology: Prefix вы- ("completely") plus пить ("to drink") — "to drink up".
commonMistakes: выпить can also be a euphemism for drinking alcohol — note the context-dependent nuance.

example.gloss: I drank a glass of water.

examples.gloss: He drank a cup of tea.

synonymComparison.note: the key contrast: пить is the ongoing act of drinking, while выпить is the perfective, 'to drink up/finish.'

past.n.gloss: Everything was drunk to the last drop.

past.pl.gloss: We each drank a glass of wine.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you have another cup?

etymology: Derived from одеть ("to dress [someone]"); the original sense was "what is worn".
commonMistakes: An uncountable collective noun used only in the singular; the plural одежды is not typical.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for repeated/ongoing "killing"; use the perfective убить for a single completed killing.
etymology: Prefix у- ("completely") plus бить ("to hit") — "to beat to death".
commonMistakes: убивать время is an idiom meaning "to kill time" — don't read it literally.

examples.gloss: He had never killed an animal.

synonymComparison.note: a synonym for 'to destroy/annihilate,' used more for inanimate/abstract objects.

past.m.gloss: He used to kill time with a book.

past.f.gloss: She used to drown out boredom with music.

past.pl.gloss: We used to spend the evening talking.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We waste the weekend at home.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You kill time at the computer.

etymology: A diminutive derived from вечер ("evening"); the original sense was "an evening gathering".
commonMistakes: More casual than праздник (a formal celebration) — it specifically means "party".

aspectUsage: Imperfective for repeated/habitual "returning"; use the perfective вернуться for a single completed return.
etymology: The imperfective derivative of вернуть, from a root meaning "to turn".
commonMistakes: Being reflexive, don't drop the -ся — and don't confuse it with the transitive возвращать ("to give back").

examples.ru: Я возвращаюсь каждый вечер в семь.
examples.gloss: I come home every evening at seven.
He came back an hour later.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: возвращаться is intransitive 'to come back oneself,' while вернуть is transitive 'to give something back.'

past.m.ru: Он возвращался каждый раз одним путём.
past.m.gloss: He always came back the same way.

past.pl.gloss: We used to come back late at night.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'm coming back to this topic.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Are you going home for the weekend?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He's falling back into old habits.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We're going back to the plan.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Are you going back to the office?

etymology: с + an oblique form of начало ("beginning") — "from the start".
commonMistakes: Don't confuse the single adverb сначала ("first/at first") with the two-word phrase с начала ("from the beginning [of something]").

aspectUsage: Imperfective for repeated/habitual "asking"; use the perfective спросить for a single completed question.
etymology: From an archaic root meaning "to ask".
commonMistakes: Note the difference between спрашивать о чём-то ("ask about something", prepositional) and спрашивать что-то ("ask [for] something", accusative).

example.gloss: He's asking me about my plans.

examples.gloss: I asked him for the address.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: спрашивать means 'to ask a question,' while просить means 'to ask for/request.'

past.m.gloss: He used to ask every day.

past.f.gloss: She was asking about his health.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Are you asking everyone?

etymology: From коло ("circle", archaic) — "around".
commonMistakes: около requires the genitive and covers both spatial "near" and quantitative "approximately".

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "departing by vehicle"; use уезжать for repeated/ongoing departure.
etymology: Prefix у- ("away") plus ехать ("to go by vehicle").
commonMistakes: Conventionally, the imperfective imperative уезжай/уезжайте is used instead, since this perfective lacks a natural imperative of its own.

examples.gloss: We left early in the morning.
The family goes away for the weekend.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: уехать is 'to leave by vehicle,' while уйти is 'to leave on foot.'

past.pl.gloss: We left the city for good.

nonpast.2pl.ru: Вы уедете на море этим летом?
nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you go to the seaside this summer?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll be away for a year.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "near".
commonMistakes: Mind the use of short forms близок/близка/близко versus the long form близкий.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed instance of "seeing each other"; use видеться for ongoing/habitual contact.
etymology: A reciprocal reflexive of видеть ("to see") — "to see one another → to meet".
commonMistakes: Being reflexive, it needs either a plural subject or с + instrumental.

examples.gloss: We saw each other after a long break.
Let's meet up on the weekend.
They see each other every week.

synonymComparison.note: увидеться ('to see each other,' slightly lighter) differs from встретиться ('to meet,' implying a more deliberate arranged meeting).

past.m.gloss: He ran into her by chance.

past.n.gloss: Everything looked different in a new light.

past.pl.gloss: We saw each other after years apart.

nonpast.3sg.ru: Он увидится с семьёй на праздники.
nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll see his family over the holidays.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you see your colleagues?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll see each other at the wedding.

imperative.pl.gloss: See each other before you leave.

aspectUsage: A stative verb ("to suppose") with no perfective counterpart.
etymology: Prefix по- plus an archaic root лагать ("to place") — "to place in the mind → to think".
commonMistakes: A fairly literary, formal verb — думать or считать are more natural in everyday speech.

examples.gloss: We suppose the plan will work.

synonymComparison.note: nearly synonymous, but полагать carries a more formal/tentative 'suppose' nuance, while считать is more assertive.

past.f.ru: Она полагала, что всё в порядке.

past.pl.gloss: We were hoping for the best.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We believe the risk is minimal.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you think this will work?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They believe the market will grow.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed instance of "turning out/working out"; use получаться for the ongoing pattern of how things turn out.
etymology: A reflexive derivative of получить — "to come out as a result".
commonMistakes: Most commonly used impersonally, as "у кого-то получилось" — first/second-person use is rare.

governance.pattern: у + genitive (for whom it worked out)

examples.gloss: We ended up with a great project.
His cooking always turns out delicious.
Drawing rarely works out for me.

synonymComparison.note: nearly synonymous but удаться leans more strongly toward success, while получиться is more neutral — 'to turn out (a certain way).'

past.n.gloss: Everything fell into place on its own.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll come out badly in the photo.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: You'll manage, I believe in you.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll end up with a great team.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You'll manage to sort everything out.

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll get everything done on time.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "stopping something"; use останавливать for repeated/ongoing stopping.
etymology: Prefix о- plus an archaic становить ("to make stand").
commonMistakes: Don't confuse the transitive остановить ("to stop something") with the intransitive остановиться ("to come to a stop").

examples.gloss: Security stops everyone at the entrance.

synonymComparison.note: a close synonym: остановить is for physically stopping something, while прекратить is for ceasing an action/process.

past.n.gloss: The decision halted the project's progress.

past.pl.gloss: We stopped the process in time.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you stop the train?

etymology: Borrowed from Greek typos ("stamp/type").
commonMistakes: Colloquially it can also mean a dismissive "weird guy" — mind the context.

etymology: Derived from связать ("to tie together").
commonMistakes: Covers both "relationship" and "communication/connection" — context decides which.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "hearing/catching something"; use слышать for the ongoing capacity to hear.
etymology: Prefix у- plus слышать ("to hear") — "to catch by hearing".
commonMistakes: Don't confuse слушать (to listen, deliberate) with слышать/услышать (to hear, perceptual).

examples.gloss: We heard footsteps outside the door.
I hear music in the distance.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: слышать/услышать is passive ('sound reaches you'), while слушать is active listening.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll hear you even from afar.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you hear us?

etymology: A fossilized instrumental form of ночь ("night"), used as an adverb.
commonMistakes: The instrumental of the noun ночь and the adverb "at night" look identical, though their function differs.

etymology: Borrowed from English "film", ultimately from Latin pellis ("skin/membrane").
commonMistakes: Distinguish кино ("movies" in general / the cinema) from фильм (an individual work).

etymology: с + an oblique form of раз ("once/time") — "in one go → right away".
commonMistakes: Besides "immediately", сразу can also mean "all at once" — mind the context.

etymology: A fossilized instrumental form of утро ("morning"), used as an adverb.
commonMistakes: The instrumental of the noun утро and the adverb "in the morning" look identical, though their function differs.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for repeated/habitual "helping"; use the perfective помочь for a single completed act of help.
etymology: Prefix по- plus an archaic могать (related to мочь, "to be able").
commonMistakes: помогать takes the dative (помогать другу, not "помогать друга").

examples.gloss: He helped me with the move.

synonymComparison.note: a more formal synonym for 'to assist/facilitate,' used in organizational/business contexts.

past.m.gloss: He used to help for free.

past.f.gloss: She used to help the kids with homework.

past.pl.gloss: We used to help the volunteers.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I help my parents around the house.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you help newcomers?

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to spread"; related to странный ("strange", originally "foreign").
commonMistakes: Distinguish страна (country/land) from государство (the state as a political entity).

etymology: A borrowing of old Germanic origin, once meaning "tower/holding place".
commonMistakes: Distinguish сидеть в тюрьме ("to be serving time", a state) from попасть в тюрьму ("to get locked up", an event).

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the habitual/ongoing act of drinking; use the perfective выпить for a single completed drink.
etymology: A basic verb tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to drink".
commonMistakes: бросить пить is an idiom meaning "to quit drinking (alcohol)" — don't read it literally.

examples.gloss: He drinks a lot of water.
We drank tea for a long time.
He drank it all at once.

synonymComparison.note: the key contrast: пить is the ongoing act of drinking, while выпить is the perfective, 'to drink up/finish.'

past.f.gloss: She drank water after her run.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you drink coffee in the mornings?

etymology: An adjective related to an archaic verb meaning "to resemble".
commonMistakes: Use похож на + accusative (not "похож с").

aspectUsage: The imperfective unidirectional verb of running. побежать is a related word meaning "to start running".
etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to flee/run".
commonMistakes: Don't confuse бежать (unidirectional) with бегать (multidirectional/habitual running).

examples.gloss: The kids took off running toward the sea.

synonymComparison.note: a related multidirectional verb: бежать is one specific directional run, while бегать is habitual/multidirectional running — the same pattern as идти/ходить.

past.m.gloss: He was running down the street.

past.f.gloss: She was running toward the exit.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Are you running with me?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They're running toward the finish line.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "eye" — "the house's eye".
commonMistakes: The plural окна is regular, but mind the genitive plural окон, which drops the ending.

etymology: Derived from решить ("to decide / to solve"); the sense is "decision/solution".
commonMistakes: Covers both "decision" and "solution [to a problem]" — context decides which.

etymology: The adverbial form of прекрасный ("wonderful").
commonMistakes: Also used alone as an exclamation of approval ("Wonderful!").

etymology: From Latin agens ("one who acts"), via French.
commonMistakes: Can mean both "spy" and "representative/agent" — context decides which.

etymology: From Old Church Slavonic тысяча, tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root for large numbers.
commonMistakes: Declines grammatically like a feminine noun; after the genitive plural тысяч, the following noun is also genitive plural.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of "introducing/representing"; use the perfective представить for a single completed introduction.
etymology: Prefix пред- ("in front") plus ставить ("to place") — "to place in front, to show".
commonMistakes: Note the reflexive idiom представлять себе ("to imagine").

example.gloss: I'm introducing a new colleague to you.

examples.gloss: He represents the company in negotiations.

synonymComparison.note: in the sense of 'to imagine,' a synonym with a more creative/fanciful nuance.

past.f.gloss: She represented the country at the Olympics.

past.pl.gloss: We were presenting the project to investors.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Do you grasp the scale of the problem?

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Can you picture the consequences?

etymology: From Old Church Slavonic обѣд, meaning "mealtime".
commonMistakes: Means "lunch" — don't confuse it with завтрак ("breakfast") or ужин ("dinner").

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of answering; use отвечать for habitual/ongoing answering.
etymology: Prefix от- plus an archaic root вет ("word") — "to give back a word → to answer".
commonMistakes: Use ответить на + accusative (not "ответить вопрос").

examples.gloss: He replied to the letter right away.

synonymComparison.note: a more specific synonym for 'to respond' (to a call, request).

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you reply to the email?

imperative.pl.gloss: Answer the questions on the form.

etymology: Derived from an archaic verb способить ("to suit"); the original sense was "a fitting way [to do something]".
commonMistakes: Nearly synonymous with метод, but способ is a more everyday, concrete "way of doing".

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to judge"; related to судить (to judge).
commonMistakes: Covers both "court (the institution)" and "trial (the process)" — context decides which.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of reading; use the perfective прочитать for finishing a read.
etymology: From Old Church Slavonic чьсти, meaning "to count / to read".
commonMistakes: Mind the aspectual difference between читать (reading as a process) and прочитать (finishing a read to the end).

examples.gloss: I read the article in full.
She read the letter out loud.

synonymComparison.note: a delimitative derivative meaning 'to read for a bit' — a short reading session rather than serious reading.

past.f.gloss: She was reading a story to the kids.

past.pl.gloss: We used to read together in the evenings.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I read the news in the morning.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He's giving a lecture to students.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you read newspapers?

imperative.pl.gloss: Read the terms of the contract.

etymology: Borrowed from French groupe, from Italian groppo.
commonMistakes: Also used for "a music band" (музыкальная группа).

etymology: A lexicalized imperative of здравствовать; the original sense is "be healthy".
commonMistakes: A formal greeting; among close friends, use привет or здравствуй (the familiar singular form).

etymology: The comparative adverb of скорый; it developed to mean "rather" as well as "faster".
commonMistakes: Carries both a "rather [than]" sense (choosing) and a "faster/sooner" sense (speed).

etymology: A natural exclamation expressing surprise or pain.
commonMistakes: Can express surprise, pain, or a sigh depending on context — don't translate it rigidly.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of sending; use отправлять for repeated/ongoing sending.
etymology: Prefix от- ("away") plus an archaic править ("to direct") — "to send off".
commonMistakes: Distinguish прислать (recipient's viewpoint, "to arrive") from отправить (sender's viewpoint, "to send off").

examples.ru: Компания отправляет товары по всей стране.
examples.gloss: The company ships goods across the country.

synonymComparison.note: nearly synonymous, but отправить tends to be used in more administrative/shipping contexts.

past.m.gloss: He sent the letter on time.

past.f.gloss: She sent money to her parents.

past.pl.gloss: We shipped the cargo by plane.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you send me a copy?

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you send a confirmation?

etymology: Developed from an emphatic form of свой ("one's own") — "genuinely one's own".
commonMistakes: Often doubled with a possessive for emphasis, as in своими собственными ("with my very own").

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "young/new".
commonMistakes: Note the short forms молод/молода/молодо used in predicate position.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "coping/managing"; use справляться for an ongoing coping process.
etymology: Prefix с- plus править ("to govern/correct") — "to handle successfully".
commonMistakes: Takes справиться с + instrumental (not "справиться задачу").

examples.gloss: He always manages on his own.

synonymComparison.note: a stronger synonym for 'to overcome' (a major difficulty).

past.f.gloss: She pulled off the role brilliantly.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll handle the new position well.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you pull off the project on time?

imperative.sg.gloss: Handle it yourself, you can do it.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of writing; use написать for a single completed piece of writing.
etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to cut/carve", from when letters were carved.
commonMistakes: Don't forget the с→ш consonant softening (пишу, пишешь...).

examples.gloss: He's been writing a book for a year.
He wrote a novel in a month.

synonymComparison.note: a more creative synonym for 'to compose' (a story, music).

past.m.gloss: He wrote poetry in his youth.

past.pl.gloss: We used to write letters to each other.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Do you write with your left hand?

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you write in English?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They write articles for the magazine.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "clear/clean".
commonMistakes: чисто случайно is an idiom meaning "purely by chance".

etymology: An old combination of с- and только, forming a quantitative adverb/pronoun.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse сколько (interrogative "how much") with столько ("this/that much").

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "covering / cloud".
commonMistakes: Note the irregular plural небеса, with an -ес- infix.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "whole/healthy"; related to исцелить ("to heal").
commonMistakes: The short forms цел/цела/цело can also mean "intact/unbroken".

etymology: The adverbial form of сильный ("strong").
commonMistakes: Also used colloquially as an intensifier meaning "very".

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "appearing"; use появляться for repeated/ongoing appearing.
etymology: Prefix по- plus явиться ("to appear").
commonMistakes: появиться на свет is an idiom meaning "to be born" — don't read it literally.

example.gloss: He showed up at the office.

synonymComparison.note: a synonym for 'to arise/emerge,' used for more abstract/non-physical occurrences.

past.n.gloss: The solution emerged on its own.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll show up in a minute.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you show up at the party?

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you show up at the meeting?

imperative.pl.gloss: All get in the photo together.

etymology: A basic word tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "mouth".
commonMistakes: Note the fleeting vowel that drops in declension (рот→рта).

etymology: Derived from ошибиться ("to make a mistake").
commonMistakes: по ошибке is a fixed instrumental phrase meaning "by mistake".

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "stopping [oneself]"; use останавливаться for repeated/ongoing stopping.
etymology: A reflexive derivative of остановить ("to stop something") — "to stop oneself".
commonMistakes: Don't confuse the intransitive остановиться ("to come to a stop") with the transitive остановить ("to stop something").

examples.gloss: The train stops at every station.
We often stop along the way.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: остановиться is intransitive 'to stop (oneself),' while остановить is transitive 'to stop something.'

past.f.gloss: She stopped to listen to the music.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you stay at a hotel?

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll stop at the gas station.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you stay with us?

etymology: A vulgar word possibly related to an archaic verb дереть ("to strip/tear").
commonMistakes: An extremely vulgar word — never use it in formal settings.

etymology: Derived from the adverb поздно ("late").
commonMistakes: A soft-stem adjective, so its neuter form is позднее (not a hard-stem *поздное).

aspectUsage: Imperfective for repeated/habitual "accepting/taking [e.g., medicine]"; use the perfective принять for a single completed act.
etymology: Prefix при- plus an archaic имать ("to take") — "to take in close → to accept".
commonMistakes: принимать решение is the standard collocation for "to make a decision".

examples.gloss: He accepted the offer right away.

synonymComparison.note: принимать ('to accept,' more formal) and брать ('to take,' general) are close but differ in nuance.

past.f.gloss: She used to make quick decisions.

past.pl.gloss: We were accepting applications until Friday.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you accept cards?

etymology: Possibly traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to burn/scorch".
commonMistakes: Mind the figurative use in expressions like чёрный юмор ("black humor").

etymology: Borrowed from Latin praesidens ("one who sits in front").
commonMistakes: As an animate noun, its accusative equals its genitive (избрать президента).

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "respect/esteem".
commonMistakes: честное слово is a fixed phrase meaning "honestly / I swear".

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing an ongoing state of worry. побеспокоиться is a related word meaning "to worry for a while" — not a true aspectual pair.
etymology: Negative prefix бес- (без-) plus покой ("calm") — "to lose one's calm".
commonMistakes: Being reflexive, don't drop the -ся; use о + prepositional for "to worry about".

examples.gloss: She always worries about her children.

synonymComparison.note: nearly synonymous, but волноваться leans more toward emotional nervousness, while беспокоиться leans toward caring concern.

past.m.gloss: He was worried about the future.

past.f.gloss: She was worried about her job.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You're worrying for no reason.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "letting go/releasing"; use отпускать for repeated/ongoing release.
etymology: Prefix от- ("away") plus пустить ("to let loose") — "to let go away".
commonMistakes: отпустить ситуацию is a figurative idiom meaning "to let go [of worrying about something]".

example.gloss: He let go of her hand.

examples.gloss: My boss let me leave early.
She let go of the grudge.

examples.ru: Он никогда не отпускает людей без причины.
examples.gloss: He never releases people without reason.
We let staff go at five.

synonymComparison.note: a stronger synonym for 'to free/liberate' from a more constraining situation.

past.m.gloss: He let go of the leash.

past.pl.gloss: We let go of the past.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you let him off for an hour?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll let the employee leave early.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll let the kids go play.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you let us leave early?

etymology: Borrowed from English "sex" (ultimately Latin sexus).
commonMistakes: An uncountable noun, used only in the singular.

etymology: Borrowed from Greek karabos ("beetle"), which developed into "ship".
commonMistakes: Note the instrumental form кораблём, with a soft stem and shifted stress.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for repeated/habitual "getting up"; use the perfective встать for a single completed act.
etymology: The imperfective derivative of встать, from the root of ставить ("to place").
commonMistakes: Covers both "to get out of bed" and "to stand up" — context decides which.

governance.pattern: with adverbs/place phrases (to get up/stand, intransitive)

examples.ru: Он встаёт в шесть каждый день.
examples.gloss: He gets up at six every day.
We get up when the alarm rings.

synonymComparison.note: a close synonym meaning 'to rise/get up,' with a broader range of use.

past.f.gloss: She used to get up before everyone else.

past.pl.gloss: We used to get up at the same time.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Do you get up this early?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He's getting up from the table.

nonpast.2pl.ru: Вы встаёте с трудом по утрам?
nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you have trouble getting up in the mornings?

imperative.pl.gloss: Get up, it's time to go.

etymology: A collective numeral derived from два ("two"), used to count people as a pair.
commonMistakes: двое is used for counting people (especially men or mixed groups); use два for objects.

etymology: Derived from выбрать ("to choose").
commonMistakes: нет выбора is a standard phrase meaning "there's no choice".

etymology: A diminutive/affectionate form of баба ("woman/old woman", colloquial).
commonMistakes: As the diminutive-affectionate form, бабушка is the standard neutral word for "grandmother" — баба by itself can sound coarse.

etymology: A natural exclamation expressing surprise, delight, or a sigh.
commonMistakes: Tends to carry a stronger note of delight/surprise than ох.

etymology: Derived from the past participle of понять ("to understand"), used as a predicate/response word.
commonMistakes: Very commonly used alone as the response "Got it".

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing an ongoing state of desire (used mainly as a 3rd-person impersonal). захотеться is its perfective partner, marking the onset of a wish.
etymology: An impersonal reflexive of хотеть ("to want"), taking a dative experiencer.
commonMistakes: In practice only the 3rd-person singular impersonal form хочется (dative construction, мне хочется = "I feel like...") is used; other persons are essentially never used.

examples.gloss: We feel like taking a walk.

synonymComparison.note: хотеть (the subject actively wants) contrasts with the impersonal хотеться (dative + 'feel like'), which is less willful/more passive.

past.m.gloss: A result like that would have been desired (literary, rare usage).

past.f.gloss: Silence was what he wanted (rare usage).

past.pl.gloss: Change was what we wanted (rare usage).

nonpast.1sg.ru: Хочусь я того или нет, придётся идти.
nonpast.1sg.gloss: Whether I want it or not, I'll have to go (rare, literary usage).

nonpast.2sg.ru: Хочешься ты этого или нет, это случится.
nonpast.2sg.gloss: Whether you want it or not, it will happen (rare usage).

nonpast.1pl.ru: Хотимся мы того или нет, решение принято.
nonpast.1pl.gloss: Whether we want it or not, the decision is made (rare usage).

nonpast.2pl.ru: Хотитесь вы или нет, правила одни для всех.
nonpast.2pl.gloss: Whether you want it or not, the rules are the same for everyone (rare usage).

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They want change, but it's scary (rare usage).

etymology: The adverbial form of довольный ("satisfied"); the sense shifted from "to the point of satisfaction" to "fairly/quite".
commonMistakes: Mind both the degree-adverb sense ("quite/fairly") and the original adjective-related sense ("satisfied").

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing recurring/occasional happening or visiting. случиться is a related word denoting a single occurrence — not a true aspectual pair.
etymology: A frequentative derivative of быть ("to be").
commonMistakes: The imperative бывай! is used colloquially as a casual farewell, "see ya".

synonymComparison.note: бывать (recurring/occasional) and случаться (a single event occurring) differ in whether the occurrence is habitual or one-time.

past.m.gloss: He used to come here often.

past.pl.gloss: We used to go there in summer.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'm sometimes busy in the mornings.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Do you ever come to this area?

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We rarely go to the theater.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you ever attend conferences?

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of naming/calling; use the imperfective называть for habitual naming.
etymology: Prefix на- plus звать ("to call").
commonMistakes: Takes the construction назвать + accusative + instrumental (назвать его героем = "call him a hero").

examples.gloss: Critics called the album a failure.
He named the price right away.

examples.ru: Они называют друг друга по кличкам.
examples.gloss: They call each other by nicknames.

synonymComparison.note: звать (to call/summon, or state a name) and назвать (to name, once) are close but used in different contexts.

past.m.ru: Он назвал сына в честь деда.
past.m.gloss: He named his son after his grandfather.

past.pl.gloss: We declared the team the winner.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you name the author?

etymology: Derived from заметить ("to notice"); the sense developed to "so good it's noticeable".
commonMistakes: Don't confuse заметный ("noticeable", simply drawing attention) with замечательный ("wonderful").

etymology: Negative prefix без- plus опасность ("danger") — "the absence of danger".
commonMistakes: Mind the без- prefix that distinguishes опасность (danger) from безопасность (safety).

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of choosing; use the imperfective выбирать for repeated/ongoing choosing.
etymology: Prefix вы- ("out") plus брать ("to take") — "to take out, to select".
commonMistakes: Don't confuse выбрать (perfective, the completed choice) with выбирать (imperfective, the process of choosing).

governance.pattern: accusative (object chosen) + из + genitive (range chosen from)

example.gloss: I chose a book from the list.

examples.gloss: I take a long time choosing gifts.

synonymComparison.note: a synonym with a stronger comparative nuance — 'to prefer' (over alternatives).

past.pl.gloss: We chose the hotel ahead of time.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you select a candidate?

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of "preparing/cooking"; use the perfective приготовить for a single completed dish.
etymology: Derived from готовый ("ready").
commonMistakes: Covers both "to cook" and "to prepare [for an exam etc.]" — context decides which.

examples.gloss: He's preparing students for the exam.
He finished making lunch on time.

synonymComparison.note: a more specific synonym for 'to boil/cook in liquid,' narrower than the general готовить.

past.f.gloss: She used to cook for the whole family.

past.pl.gloss: We were preparing a festive dinner.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He's preparing a report for the meeting.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you make the dish yourself?

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of noticing; use замечать for ongoing noticing/observing.
etymology: Prefix за- plus метить ("to mark") — "to mark and notice".
commonMistakes: Mind the difference between the verb заметить ("to notice") and the derived noun замечание ("a remark/comment").

examples.gloss: She noticed the change right away.
We spotted him in the crowd.

examples.ru: Я не замечаю времени, когда работаю.
examples.gloss: I lose track of time when I work.

synonymComparison.note: заметить ('to notice,' attention-focused) is close to увидеть ('to see,' visual perception), but заметить carries a stronger attentiveness nuance.

past.m.gloss: He noticed the change in behavior.

past.f.ru: Она заметила грусть в его глазах.
past.f.gloss: She noticed sadness in his eyes.

past.pl.gloss: We noticed the problem in time.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll notice the mistake right away.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You'll notice the difference in quality.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root for the numeral "four".
commonMistakes: Unlike numerals 5 and above, 2/3/4 are followed by the singular genitive (четыре часа).

etymology: An adverb from an old case form of пред- ("before") — "formerly".
commonMistakes: прежде всего is a fixed phrase meaning "first of all".

etymology: An abstract noun derived from возможный ("possible").
commonMistakes: Distinguish шанс (a chance occurrence) from возможность (possibility/opportunity).

etymology: A euphonic variant of the preposition о, used before мне and a few other pronouns.
commonMistakes: обо is used specifically before мне — a special euphonic form.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin informatio.
commonMistakes: An uncountable noun used only in the singular; the plural информации is unusual.

etymology: Derived from интересовать ("to interest").
commonMistakes: The short forms интересен/интересна/интересно are used in predicate position.

etymology: From Latin camera ("chamber"); covers both "camera (device)" and "cell (prison)".
commonMistakes: Covers both "camera" and "prison cell" — context decides which.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of introducing/presenting; use представлять for the ongoing process.
etymology: Prefix пред- plus ставить ("to place").
commonMistakes: Note the reflexive idiom представить себе ("to imagine").

example.gloss: I introduced my friend to my colleagues.

examples.gloss: He presented the project to investors.

synonymComparison.note: представить ('to present formally') is close to показать ('to show,' more direct) but used in different contexts.

past.m.gloss: He submitted the report to the commission.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll present the plan to you.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you introduce me to your friends?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll unveil the new product line.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you represent the company at the exhibition?

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of explaining; use объяснять for repeated/ongoing explaining.
etymology: Prefix об- plus ясный ("clear") — "to make clear".
commonMistakes: Use объяснить + accusative (not "объяснить о проблеме").

example.gloss: He explained the rule to me.

examples.gloss: She explained the situation in detail.
The teacher explained the topic clearly.

examples.ru: Я объясняю это снова и снова.
examples.gloss: I keep explaining this over and over.

synonymComparison.note: a synonym for 'to clarify/elucidate thoroughly,' a more exhaustive explanation.

past.f.gloss: She explained the rules of the game.

past.pl.gloss: We explained the terms of the contract.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll explain everything to you later.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you explain this to me?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll explain the process in detail.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll explain everything at the meeting.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you explain your position?

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to measure".
commonMistakes: принять меры is a fixed idiom meaning "to take measures/action".

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed instance of "getting acquainted"; use знакомиться for the ongoing process.
etymology: Prefix по- plus знакомиться ("to become acquainted").
commonMistakes: Being reflexive, it needs с + instrumental (познакомиться с другом = "to meet/get to know a friend").

example.gloss: I got acquainted with a colleague.

examples.ru: Он знакомится с новыми людьми легко.

examples.gloss: We're getting acquainted with the country's culture.

synonymComparison.note: the key difference: познакомиться specifically means meeting for the first time, while встретиться ('to meet') can apply to people who already know each other.

past.f.gloss: She got to know the city.

nonpast.3sg.ru: Он познакомится с командой на этой неделе.
nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll meet the team this week.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you meet the new director?

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of passing on/conveying; use передавать for repeated/ongoing conveying.
etymology: Prefix пере- plus дать ("to give") — "to give across".
commonMistakes: передать привет is the fixed phrase for "say hi [to someone] for me".

examples.gloss: She passed on greetings to her parents.
We referred the case to court.
The radio broadcasts news every hour.
He passes on his experience to younger colleagues.

synonymComparison.note: a more formal synonym for 'to hand over/present' (at a ceremony).

past.m.gloss: He handed over power to his successor.

past.f.gloss: She delivered the message on time.

past.pl.gloss: We passed knowledge on to the next generation.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you hand me the keys?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll deliver the application to the office.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll hand off the project to the team.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you pass the information to colleagues?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll hand over the business to the new director.

imperative.pl.gloss: Pass my words on to everyone.

etymology: A lexicalized neuter short form of интересный ("interesting"), used as an impersonal predicate.
commonMistakes: Distinguish the adjective интересный from the impersonal predicate интересно ("it is interesting that...").

etymology: за + an instrumental form of тот — "after that".
commonMistakes: затем is more literary/formal than потом.

etymology: An agent noun derived from учить ("to teach").
commonMistakes: Distinguish преподаватель (a lecturer, university level) from учитель (mainly a school teacher).

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "early".
commonMistakes: Don't confuse it with its comparative раньше ("earlier" / "before, in the past").

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "flat surface".
commonMistakes: This spelling is also a homograph for "gender/sex" — a completely different word (this entry covers "floor"). Note the special locative form полу used in "на полу".

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of telling/narrating; use the perfective рассказать for a single completed telling.
etymology: Prefix рас- plus an archaic казать ("to show") — "to show in detail → to narrate".
commonMistakes: Typically takes о + prepositional (though direct accusative is also possible depending on the object).

examples.gloss: Grandma tells fairy tales in the evenings.

examples.ru: Он рассказывает о поездке с удовольствием.
examples.gloss: He talks about the trip with pleasure.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: рассказывать means to narrate/tell a story in detail, while говорить means to simply say something.

past.f.gloss: She used to talk about her childhood.

past.n.gloss: The radio reported the news every hour.

past.pl.gloss: We used to tell each other secrets.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Are you telling everyone about this?

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We tell customers about the product.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Are you talking about your experience?

etymology: во + an old demonstrative он — "over there".
commonMistakes: Points to something farther away than вот.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "back".
commonMistakes: повернуться спиной is also used figuratively, meaning "to turn one's back on [someone]".

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to sleep"; related to спать (to sleep).
commonMistakes: Covers both "sleep" and "a dream" — context decides which.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "high place".
commonMistakes: гора проблем is a figurative idiom meaning "a mountain of problems".

etymology: A colloquial shortening of чтобы.
commonMistakes: More colloquial/casual-sounding than чтобы.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of paying; use платить for habitual/ongoing paying.
etymology: Prefix за- plus платить ("to pay").
commonMistakes: Use заплатить за + accusative (not "заплатить ужин").

examples.gloss: He paid the tax on time.
She paid the fine right away.

synonymComparison.note: a more administrative synonym for 'to settle payment' (a bill, invoice).

past.f.gloss: She paid with a credit card.

past.pl.gloss: We paid for the tickets in advance.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll pay off the debt in full.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you pay for delivery?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll pay the fine on time.

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing ongoing "holding on/behaving". продержаться is a related word meaning "to hold out for a while" — not a true aspectual pair.
etymology: A reflexive derivative of держать ("to hold") — "to hold oneself".
commonMistakes: Takes держаться за + accusative (держаться за руку = "to hold [someone's] hand").

examples.ru: Мы держимся вместе в трудные времена.
examples.gloss: We stick together in hard times.

synonymComparison.note: a synonym for 'to endure/put up with,' implying a more painful kind of persistence.

past.n.gloss: Everything held together on a mere promise.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Are you clinging to old habits?

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You're holding up well.

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They're sticking to their version of events.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "taking off/removing"; use снимать for repeated/ongoing removing.
etymology: Prefix с- ("down/off") plus an archaic ять ("to take") — "to take off".
commonMistakes: Mind the polysemy: снять фильм means "to shoot a film", снять квартиру means "to rent an apartment".

example.gloss: He took the jacket off the hook.

examples.gloss: The director shot a new film.
I take off my shoes at the door.

synonymComparison.note: a more administrative/legal synonym for 'to rent/lease,' with a more contractual ring than снять.

past.f.gloss: She withdrew money from the account.

past.pl.gloss: We booked a room at the hotel.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll withdraw money in the morning.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you take off your jacket?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll rent an apartment for a year.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll shoot a video on the phone.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Would you take off your shoes at the entrance?

etymology: The adverbial form of странный ("strange").
commonMistakes: Also used alone as an exclamation ("That's strange").

etymology: A natural exclamation expressing surprise or pain.
commonMistakes: Used for a mild surprise or small pain, lighter in tone than ох.

etymology: Borrowed from English "hello" or French allô; used specifically to answer the phone.
commonMistakes: Used only when picking up the phone, not as a face-to-face greeting.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "calming down"; use успокаиваться for the ongoing process of calming.
etymology: Prefix у- plus покой ("calm") — "to regain one's calm".
commonMistakes: The imperative успокойся! is a common everyday phrase, "calm down!"

governance.pattern: used with adverbs/context (to calm down, intransitive)

examples.gloss: She calmed down after the talk.
The sea calmed down by evening.
The kids settle down before bed.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: успокоиться is intransitive 'to calm down (oneself),' while успокоить is transitive 'to calm someone else down.'

past.m.gloss: He didn't calm down right away.

past.f.gloss: She calmed down an hour later.

past.pl.gloss: We calmed down after the news.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll calm down once it's all over.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll calm down once he sees the result.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you calm down if I explain?

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "shared".
commonMistakes: в общем is a fixed adverbial phrase meaning "in general/basically".

etymology: An old combination of один and раз ("once") — "one time".
commonMistakes: A literary adverb frequently used to open a story.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "foreign" (related to страна); the sense shifted from "alien" to "strange".
commonMistakes: Note the shared root with страна ("country"), though the meanings diverge sharply.

etymology: The adverbial form of обычный ("usual").
commonMistakes: как обычно is a fixed phrase meaning "as usual".

etymology: Derived from ужас ("horror").
commonMistakes: Also used colloquially as a strong intensifier ("terribly bad").

etymology: Borrowed from Italian millione, an augmentative of mille ("thousand").
commonMistakes: миллион раз is a figurative emphatic phrase meaning "countless times".

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "open/spread-out place".
commonMistakes: поле деятельности is a figurative collocation meaning "field of activity".

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of catching; use ловить for repeated/ongoing catching.
etymology: Prefix по- plus an archaic ять ("to take") — "to take and catch".
commonMistakes: поймать на слове is a figurative idiom meaning "to catch [someone] in a contradiction".

examples.gloss: The kids are catching butterflies in the garden.

synonymComparison.note: a synonym for a more sudden/forceful grab — 'to seize/grab.'

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll make his flight on time.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you get signal here?

etymology: Derived from мыслить ("to think").
commonMistakes: Distinguish идея (an idea/notion) from мысль (a thought).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin advocatus ("one called to help/defend").
commonMistakes: As an animate noun, its accusative equals its genitive (нанять адвоката).

etymology: The plural form of другой, lexicalized as its own determiner.
commonMistakes: Mind the number contrast: другой (singular, "another") versus другие (plural, "others").

etymology: ин- ("other") plus an old manner suffix — "in another way".
commonMistakes: Mind both senses: "differently" and the conditional "otherwise [if not...]".

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "taking something up"; use заниматься for the ongoing engagement.
etymology: Prefix за- plus an archaic ять ("to take") in reflexive form — "to take oneself up with".
commonMistakes: Takes заняться + instrumental (заняться спортом, not "заняться спорт").

examples.gloss: We got right to work on the project.
I've been doing translation work for a year.

synonymComparison.note: a synonym with a stronger 'getting down to' nuance — 'to take on' a task.

past.m.gloss: He got down to the matter seriously.

past.f.gloss: She set about solving the problem.

past.n.gloss: Everything started moving on its own.

past.pl.gloss: We got to work renovating the house.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you take on the report?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll take charge of the organization.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you handle the accounting?

etymology: Borrowed from Greek systema ("a whole compounded of parts").
commonMistakes: Distinguish структура (structure) from система (a system/scheme).

etymology: Derived from согласиться ("to agree") — "in agreement"; also used as the phonetics term for "consonant".
commonMistakes: Carries two very different senses — "in agreement (a person)" versus "a consonant (a letter)" — mind the context.

etymology: Derived from петь ("to sing").
commonMistakes: Note the irregular genitive plural песен, with a dropped ending and fleeting vowel.

etymology: A lexicalized neuter short form of приятный ("pleasant", from an archaic verb приять, "to accept").
commonMistakes: приятно познакомиться is a fixed phrase used when meeting someone for the first time — learn it as a whole unit.

etymology: A basic word tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "tree".
commonMistakes: Note the irregular plural деревья, with a -ев- infix.

etymology: Derived from пить ("to drink"); the original sense is "a drink".
commonMistakes: Normally singular as an uncountable noun, but a plural can refer to different "types" of beer.

etymology: Derived from сообщить ("to inform").
commonMistakes: Covers both "message" and "announcement/report" — context decides which.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of "sounding/resonating"; use прозвучать for a single completed instance.
etymology: Derived from звук ("sound").
commonMistakes: Often used figuratively to mean "to come across as" (звучит странно = "that sounds strange").

examples.gloss: A shot rang out in the silence.
Her words came across as convincing.

synonymComparison.note: звучать is specific to how something sounds (audibly), while казаться is the general 'to seem/appear' across any impression.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You sound upset.

etymology: Borrowed from German Ziel.
commonMistakes: с какой целью ("for what purpose") is a standard question phrase.

etymology: Borrowed from English "detective"; carries both the "detective (person)" and "detective story" senses.
commonMistakes: Covers both "a detective" and "a detective novel/show" — context decides which.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cursus ("a running / a course").
commonMistakes: Polysemous — "course (class)", "direction/heading", "exchange rate" — mind the context.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "marrow/spinal cord".
commonMistakes: вынести мозг is a colloquial idiom meaning "to drive someone crazy with nagging".

etymology: Derived from лечить ("to treat/cure").
commonMistakes: A general word for "medicine", distinct from таблетка (a pill, a specific form).

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "making no sound".
commonMistakes: немой фильм is the historical term for "a silent film".

etymology: From the name of Charlemagne (Karl), which spread into Slavic languages generally as a word for "king".
commonMistakes: Distinguish царь (the specifically Russian title "tsar") from король (a European-style "king").

etymology: об- plus an archaic рат ("to turn back") — "back to where one started".
commonMistakes: Distinguish назад ("backward" / "ago") from обратно ("back to the original place").

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of placing/setting; use ставить for repeated/ongoing placing.
etymology: Prefix по- plus ставить ("to place").
commonMistakes: поставить вопрос/цель are figurative collocations meaning "to raise a question / set a goal".

example.gloss: I put the vase on the table.

examples.gloss: He parked the car in the garage.

examples.ru: Я всегда ставлю будильник на семь.
examples.gloss: I always set my alarm for seven.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: поставить is for placing something upright/standing, while положить is for placing something lying flat.

past.n.ru: Решение поставило всё на свои места.
past.n.gloss: The decision put everything back in order.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you raise the issue directly?

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of dropping by/entering; use заходить for repeated/ongoing visits.
etymology: Prefix за- plus идти ("to go") — "to step briefly inside".
commonMistakes: зайти в гости is a standard colloquial collocation for "to drop by/visit".

examples.gloss: He stopped by for a minute.
The sun set behind the mountains.
He often stops by the café.

synonymComparison.note: a synonym for 'to pop in/run by briefly,' implying more haste.

past.m.gloss: He stopped by the office in passing.

past.pl.ru: Мы зашли в бар после работы.
past.pl.gloss: We stopped by the bar after work.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you stop by my place?

nonpast.3sg.ru: Он зайдёт в банк по дороге.
nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll stop at the bank on the way.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll drop in for a minute.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you come by our place?

imperative.sg.gloss: Come by my place after work.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of changing [something]; use изменять for repeated/ongoing changing.
etymology: Prefix из- plus an archaic менить ("to change").
commonMistakes: Don't confuse изменить (transitive, "to change something") with измениться (intransitive, "to change/become different").

examples.ru: Он никогда не изменяет своим принципам.
examples.gloss: He never betrays his own principles.

synonymComparison.note: nearly synonymous, but поменять is more colloquial/everyday for 'swap/change.'

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll change the terms of the contract.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you change the company's policy?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll change the rules of the game.

etymology: Derived from править ("to govern/guide").
commonMistakes: золотое правило is a fixed idiom meaning "the golden rule".

etymology: Derived from an archaic приять ("to accept"); the original sense is "one who is liked / a buddy".
commonMistakes: A bit more casual than друг — closer to "pal/buddy/acquaintance".

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing an ongoing state of "trusting". довериться is a related stative word meaning "to place oneself in [someone's] hands" — not a true aspectual pair.
etymology: Prefix до- plus верить ("to believe") — "to believe fully".
commonMistakes: Takes доверять + dative (доверять другу, not "доверять друга").

synonymComparison.note: доверять ('to trust,' more relational) differs from верить ('to believe,' broader — believing something is true).

past.n.gloss: Everything was entrusted to his experience.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you trust this data?

aspectUsage: Imperfective for repeated/habitual "answering / being responsible"; use the perfective ответить for a single completed answer.
etymology: Prefix от- plus an archaic вет ("word").
commonMistakes: отвечать за + accusative carries the separate meaning "to be responsible for".

synonymComparison.note: a more specific synonym for 'to respond' (to a call, request).

past.f.gloss: She was responsible for the whole department.

past.n.gloss: Everything lived up to his expectations.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He's in charge of the team.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Are you in charge of hosting guests?

etymology: на + сколько ("how much") — an interrogative/exclamatory adverb.
commonMistakes: насколько я знаю is a fixed phrase meaning "as far as I know".

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of moving; use the perfective двинуться for a single completed start of movement.
etymology: A reflexive derivative of двигать ("to move something").
commonMistakes: Covers both literal physical movement and the figurative "to make progress".

examples.gloss: We set off in the morning.

synonymComparison.note: a more formal/technical synonym for 'to move/relocate.'

past.n.gloss: Everything was moving in the same direction.

past.pl.gloss: We were moving toward our goal.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: The sun moves across the sky.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We're moving in the right direction.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You're moving toward success.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "light [in weight]".
commonMistakes: Covers both "light (weight)" and "easy (difficulty)" — context decides which.

etymology: Derived from писать ("to write"); the original sense is "something written".
commonMistakes: Mind the irregular genitive plural писем, with a dropped ending.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "value/worth".
commonMistakes: Distinguish цена ("price") from стоимость ("cost/value").

aspectUsage: Imperfective for repeated/habitual "shooting"; use the perfective выстрелить for a single completed shot.
etymology: Derived from стрела ("arrow"); the original sense is "to shoot an arrow".
commonMistakes: Takes стрелять в + accusative (стрелять в цель = "to shoot at a target").

example.gloss: He was shooting at the target.

examples.gloss: The soldiers were shooting from a distance.
The guard fired into the air.

synonymComparison.note: a more colloquial/rough synonym for 'to blast away' indiscriminately.

past.pl.ru: Мы стреляли по целям на тренировке.
past.pl.gloss: We were shooting at targets in training.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Do you shoot with a pistol?

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you shoot a bow?

etymology: Borrowed from French situation, ultimately from Latin situs ("position").
commonMistakes: Distinguish положение (one's standing/circumstances) from ситуация (a concrete situation/event).

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing process of "becoming"; use the perfective стать for a single completed change.
etymology: The imperfective derivative of стать.
commonMistakes: Takes становиться + instrumental (становиться врачом = "to become a doctor").

synonymComparison.note: a synonym for a more dramatic transformation — 'to turn into' something entirely different.

past.pl.ru: Мы становились ближе друг к другу.
past.pl.gloss: We were growing closer to each other.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: You're starting to look like your father.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You're gaining more experience.

etymology: Likely a Turkic borrowing, which came to be used alongside the older Slavic root пёс.
commonMistakes: Distinguish пёс (masculine, somewhat casual) from собака (feminine, the standard neutral word regardless of the dog's sex).

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "shining/white".
commonMistakes: белый флаг is a figurative idiom meaning "surrender".

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing the state of "standing"; it has no true perfective counterpart (постоять is a related word meaning "to stand for a while").
etymology: A basic verb tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to stand".
commonMistakes: стоять в очереди is the standard collocation for "to stand in line".

example.gloss: I'm standing at the bus stop.

examples.gloss: The house stands on a hill.
The car is parked in front of the entrance.
Let's stand here for a bit.
He stood for a minute and left.

synonymComparison.note: стоять ('to stand,' implying posture) is close to находиться ('to be located,' more general, posture-neutral).

past.f.gloss: She was standing by the window.

past.pl.gloss: We stood in line for an hour.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He stands at the head of the company.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You're first on the list.

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They stand guard over the law.

etymology: Derived from the root of образовать ("to form"); the original sense is "shape/form".
commonMistakes: образ жизни is a standard collocation meaning "lifestyle".

etymology: An item-of-clothing noun possibly related etymologically to платить ("to pay" — cloth once served as currency).
commonMistakes: The plural genitive платьев is regular, but mind the spelling.

etymology: Derived from an archaic уречь ("to prescribe"); the original sense is "an assigned task".
commonMistakes: извлечь урок is a figurative idiom meaning "to learn a lesson".

etymology: Borrowed from English "dollar", ultimately from German Taler.
commonMistakes: After 2-4 the singular genitive доллара is used; after 5+ the plural genitive долларов.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cliens ("one under protection").
commonMistakes: As an animate noun, its accusative equals its genitive (обслужить клиента).

etymology: Borrowed from English "computer", ultimately from Latin computare ("to calculate").
commonMistakes: "To work at the computer" is работать за компьютером (instrumental + за).

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "getting/reaching for something"; use доставать for repeated/ongoing reaching.
etymology: Prefix до- plus an archaic стать ("to reach") — "to reach and take".
commonMistakes: Also used colloquially to mean "to annoy/pester" (Ты меня достал! = "You're driving me crazy").

example.gloss: He took the book out of his bag.

examples.gloss: She got the tickets in advance.
We got hold of a rare book.
I take out the documents every time.

examples.ru: Он достаёт деньги с трудом в последнее время.
examples.gloss: He's been struggling to get money lately.

synonymComparison.note: достать ('to obtain with effort,' implying scarcity) differs from получить ('to receive,' more neutral).

past.m.gloss: He took his phone out of his pocket.

past.f.gloss: She took the keys out of her bag.

past.n.gloss: Everything got on my nerves to the limit.

past.pl.gloss: We got hold of the contacts we needed.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll get that from the shelf.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll get hold of money temporarily.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you manage to get concert tickets?

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "voice/to call".
commonMistakes: подать голос is a figurative idiom meaning "to vote / to voice an opinion".

etymology: Derived from разговаривать ("to converse").
commonMistakes: Distinguish беседа (a formal conversation) from разговор (an everyday conversation) by register.

etymology: к plus an archaic стать ("to suit") — "at a fitting moment".
commonMistakes: кстати говоря is a standard phrase for shifting topic, "by the way".

etymology: Borrowed from Greek krabbatos, meaning "bed/couch".
commonMistakes: Distinguish кровать (the bed frame/furniture) from постель (the bedding/bed as a whole).

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "shutting up" (very colloquial/rude). Use затыкаться for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: Prefix за- plus an archaic derivative of ткнуться ("to poke/jab") — "to plug one's mouth".
commonMistakes: The imperative заткнись! is very rude — never use it outside close, informal relationships.

governance.pattern: used with adverbs/context (to shut up, intransitive, colloquial/rude)

examples.ru: Все замолчали, и он заткнулся тоже.
examples.gloss: Everyone fell silent, and he shut up too.
Sometimes it's better to shut up and listen.

synonymComparison.note: a more polite/neutral synonym for 'to fall silent'; заткнуться carries a very rude, blunt tone.

past.f.gloss: She went silent out of hurt.

past.n.gloss: Everything went silent for a second.

past.pl.gloss: We went quiet when we heard the noise.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll shut up if you ask.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll shut up once he understands.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll be quiet for a while.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Would you shut up, please (rude)?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll shut up on their own.

etymology: Derived from перевести ("to translate / to transfer").
commonMistakes: Covers both "translation" and "[money] transfer" — context decides which.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "figuring out/sorting out"; use разбираться for the ongoing process.
etymology: Prefix раз- plus a variant of собраться ("to gather") — "to take apart and sort out".
commonMistakes: Takes разобраться в + prepositional (разобраться в проблеме).

examples.ru: Я разбираюсь с почтой каждое утро.
examples.gloss: I sort through mail every morning.

synonymComparison.note: разобраться ('to figure out through careful examination') differs from понять ('to understand,' more general) in the depth of the process.

past.m.gloss: He figured it all out himself.

past.f.gloss: She sorted things out with her colleagues.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you figure out the settings?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll figure out the code quickly.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you handle the complaint?

etymology: A basic word tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "nose".
commonMistakes: The special locative form на носу ("right nearby, imminent") is used for "close at hand"; also note idioms like водить за нос ("to deceive someone").

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of "spending [time] / seeing someone off / conducting"; use провести for a single completed instance.
etymology: Prefix про- plus водить ("to lead").
commonMistakes: Polysemous — "to spend time", "to see someone off/escort", "to hold an event" — mind the context.

example.gloss: I spend time with my family.

synonymComparison.note: a synonym with more of a 'spend/expend' nuance (time, money).

past.m.gloss: He used to spend evenings reading.

past.n.gloss: Everything was conducted according to plan.

past.pl.gloss: We used to conduct research regularly.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Do you spend a lot of time online?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He runs training sessions for newcomers.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you spend your time productively?

etymology: Derived from списать ("to copy down").
commonMistakes: Nearly synonymous with перечень ("enumeration"), but список is the more common everyday word.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for repeated/habitual joking; use the perfective пошутить for a single completed joke.
etymology: Derived from шутка ("a joke").
commonMistakes: Takes шутить над + instrumental (шутить над другом = "to tease a friend").

governance.pattern: над + instrumental (to joke at someone's expense)

examples.gloss: She always jokes around in meetings.

examples.ru: Мы шутим друг с другом постоянно.
examples.gloss: We constantly joke with each other.

synonymComparison.note: a related word with a different role: шутить is the active 'to joke,' while смеяться is the responsive 'to laugh.'

past.n.gloss: Jokes came easily in that group.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Are you seriously joking?

imperative.pl.gloss: Be more careful with your jokes.

etymology: A basic word tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "sun".
commonMistakes: The л is silent in pronunciation (солнце is pronounced [so-ntse]).

etymology: когда ("when") plus the indefinite particle -нибудь — "someday".
commonMistakes: Used in questions/conditionals for an indefinite future; in plain positive statements однажды can sound more natural.

aspectUsage: A perfective related word meaning "to wait a little" (delimitative). ждать is the general imperfective "to wait" — not a true aspectual pair.
etymology: Prefix по- plus an archaic годить ("to wait for the right moment").
commonMistakes: The imperative погоди! is a very common everyday way to say "hold on!"

governance.pattern: used with adverbs/context (to wait a bit, intransitive, colloquial)

synonymComparison.note: nearly synonymous, but подождать is the standard, widely used verb; погодить is colloquial and mostly seen in the imperative.

past.n.gloss: Everything was put off until morning.

past.pl.gloss: We held off on the purchase.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll hold off on the final decision.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Would you wait a bit?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll hold off on their reply.

etymology: Borrowed from Italian bambagia ("cotton"); the original reference was to paper made from cotton.
commonMistakes: Normally singular as an uncountable noun, but бумаги (plural) is used for "documents/papers".

etymology: Borrowed from Latin operatio ("a work/operation").
commonMistakes: Covers both "surgical operation" and "[military/financial] operation" — context decides which.

etymology: Derived from звонить ("to ring / to call").
commonMistakes: Note the fleeting vowel that drops in declension (звонок→звонка).

etymology: A basic word tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "egg".
commonMistakes: Mind the irregular genitive plural яиц.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for repeated/habitual selling; use the perfective продать for a single completed sale.
etymology: Prefix про- plus давать ("to give") — "to hand over and sell".
commonMistakes: Mind the aspect pair продавать (selling, ongoing) versus продать (to complete a sale).

examples.gloss: She sells jewelry at the exhibition.

synonymComparison.note: a more general synonym for 'to trade/do business.'

past.m.gloss: He used to sell vegetables at the market.

past.f.gloss: She used to sell books at the shop.

past.pl.gloss: We used to sell tickets at the entrance.

nonpast.1pl.ru: Мы продаём продукцию по всей стране.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you sell secondhand items?

etymology: A nominalized adjective from the future stem of быть ("to be") — "that which is to come".
commonMistakes: This is the neuter form of the adjective будущий ("future") used as a noun, so it declines like an adjective.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of entering; use входить for repeated/ongoing entering.
etymology: Prefix во- plus идти ("to go") — "to go into".
commonMistakes: войти в историю is a figurative idiom meaning "to go down in history".

examples.gloss: The company entered a new market.
Guests enter through the main entrance.
This is included in the price.

synonymComparison.note: войти ('to enter,' fully) differs from зайти ('to drop in,' briefly) in purpose and duration.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll go in in a minute.

nonpast.3sg.ru: Он войдёт в курс дела быстро.
nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll get up to speed quickly.

nonpast.1pl.ru: Мы войдём в зал через дверь.
nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll enter the hall through the door.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you join the committee?

nonpast.3pl.ru: Они войдут в историю как первые.
nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll go down in history as the first.

etymology: The plural of некоторый ("some"), used as its own determiner.
commonMistakes: Distinguish некоторый from несколько, which emphasizes a small quantity.

etymology: Derived from покоиться ("to rest/be at peace").
