commonMistakes: The short forms спокоен/спокойна/спокойно are commonly used in predicate position.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of placing; use класть for repeated/ongoing placing.
etymology: Prefix по- plus an archaic ложить ("to place").
commonMistakes: Note that положить (perfective) and класть (imperfective) have completely different stems — an irregular aspectual pair.

example.gloss: I put the book on the table.

examples.gloss: She deposited the money in the bank.
I always put my keys here.
He puts sugar in his tea.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: положить is for placing something lying flat, while поставить is for placing something upright/standing.

past.m.gloss: He put an end to the argument.

past.f.gloss: She laid the foundation for the project.

past.n.gloss: Everything was put back in place.

past.pl.gloss: We put the documents in the folder.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll put the things in the closet.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll put an end to this.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll lay the groundwork for the future.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you put money into the account?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll put the goods on the shelves.

imperative.pl.gloss: Put the things back in place.

etymology: Derived from the root of ехать ("to go by vehicle"); the original sense is "a line that travels".
commonMistakes: Mind the irregular plural поезда, with a stress shift.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of "passing through / elapsing"; use the perfective пройти for a single completed pass.
etymology: Prefix про- plus ходить ("to walk") — "to walk past".
commonMistakes: проходить обучение is a figurative collocation meaning "to undergo training".

example.gloss: The road passes through the forest.

synonymComparison.note: a more literary synonym for 'to pass' (a danger, a period of time).

past.m.gloss: He used to walk past every day.

past.pl.gloss: We used to walk this route before.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: The lesson is held in this hall.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Are you going through an interview today?

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "simple/spread out".
commonMistakes: The short forms прост/проста/просто are used in predicate position.

etymology: Derived from an archaic преступить ("to step over/transgress"); the original sense is "transgressing the law".
commonMistakes: Unlike грех (a religious sin), преступление specifically denotes a legal crime.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "forest/thicket".
commonMistakes: The phrase "в лесу" uses a special second locative form лесу.

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing an ongoing state of ability. научиться is a related word meaning "to become able to [do something]" — not a true aspectual pair.
etymology: Derived from the root of ум ("intellect") — "to be able through intellect".
commonMistakes: Distinguish уметь (to be able, as a learned skill) from мочь (to be able, situationally).

examples.gloss: She knows how to play the piano.
They know how to work as a team.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: уметь means 'to know how to' (a learned skill), while мочь means 'to be able to' in a more general/situational sense.

past.f.gloss: She knew how to persuade people.

past.pl.gloss: We knew how to find solutions.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Do you know how to ski?

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We know how to adapt quickly.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Can you work under pressure?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They know how to find common ground.

imperative.pl.gloss: Learn to listen to each other.

etymology: An archaic demonstrative determiner tracing to a Proto-Indo-European demonstrative root, surviving today only in fixed expressions.
commonMistakes: Barely used in modern Russian outside the archaic set phrase по сей день ("to this day").

etymology: Derived from родить ("to give birth").
commonMistakes: день рождения is the essential fixed phrase for "birthday".

etymology: Borrowed from French billet; the original sense is "a small slip of paper/note".
commonMistakes: обратный билет refers to the return leg of a round-trip ticket.

etymology: A basic word tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to cut".
commonMistakes: The instrumental form is ножом, following the regular hard-stem masculine pattern.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of stealing; use красть for repeated/ongoing stealing.
etymology: Prefix у- ("completely") plus красть ("to steal").
commonMistakes: украсть время is a figurative idiom meaning "to steal/waste someone's time".

example.gloss: He stole a wallet from a tourist.

examples.ru: В этом районе часто крадут велосипеды.
examples.gloss: Bicycles are often stolen in this area.

synonymComparison.note: a stronger synonym for 'to abduct/steal' something more serious, including kidnapping.

past.m.gloss: He stole money from the register.

past.f.gloss: She stole a moment of glory.

past.n.gloss: Everything was stolen in one night.

past.pl.ru: Мы украли немного времени для отпуска.
past.pl.gloss: We carved out some time for vacation.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll steal a minute of your time.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Are you going to steal his idea?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll steal the chance from others.

nonpast.1pl.ru: Мы украдём немного времени на себя.
nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll carve out some time for ourselves.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Are you going to steal our audience?

etymology: Derived from глава ("head/chapter"); the original sense is "at the head / most important".
commonMistakes: самое главное is a standard nominalized phrase meaning "the most important thing".

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of approaching/suiting; use подходить for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: Prefix по- ("approach") plus до- ("reach") plus идти ("to go").
commonMistakes: Covers both "to come closer" and "to suit/fit [a requirement]" — context decides which.

example.gloss: He walked up to the window.

examples.gloss: He's approaching the end of the project.

synonymComparison.note: a more formal synonym for 'to draw near/approach' physically.

past.m.gloss: He walked up to the door.

nonpast.1sg.ru: Я подойду к тебе через минуту.
nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll come over to you in a minute.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you pick up the phone?

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you come over to us?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll approach the end of their shift.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of watching/monitoring; use the perfective проследить for a single completed act of tracking.
etymology: Derived from след ("footprint"); the original sense is "to follow a trail".
commonMistakes: Takes следить за + instrumental (следить за ребёнком = "to watch over a child").

examples.gloss: He traced the whole route of the package.
We traced the source of the problem.

synonymComparison.note: a more neutral/academic synonym for 'to observe.'

past.n.gloss: Everything seemed to be watching what was happening.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I keep an eye on my health.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Are you keeping track of the schedule?

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you follow trends?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They monitor compliance with the rules.

imperative.pl.gloss: Keep an eye on your luggage.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of ending; use заканчиваться for the ongoing process of ending.
etymology: A reflexive derivative of закончить — "to end by itself".
commonMistakes: Don't confuse the intransitive закончиться ("to come to an end") with the transitive закончить ("to finish something").

examples.gloss: The deadline is coming up soon.

synonymComparison.note: nearly synonymous but more formal/business-like for 'to be completed.'

past.m.gloss: The match ended in a draw.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: (rare usage) I will end ahead of schedule.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: (rare usage) When will you be done with work?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: The project will finish on time.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: (rare usage) We will end on time.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: (rare usage) Will you be done today?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: Supplies will run out by winter.

etymology: Derived from лицо ("person/face"); the original sense is "pertaining to the individual".
commonMistakes: личная жизнь is a standard collocation meaning "private life".

aspectUsage: Imperfective for repeated/habitual receiving; use the perfective получить for a single completed receipt.
etymology: Prefix по- plus an archaic лучати ("to obtain").
commonMistakes: получать удовольствие is a figurative collocation meaning "to enjoy [something]".

examples.gloss: She receives support from her family.

synonymComparison.note: a more formal synonym for 'to acquire.'

past.n.gloss: Everything used to work out easily.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He gets a bonus every year.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you get a discount?

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "arranging/getting [someone] set up"; use устраивать for repeated/ongoing arranging.
etymology: Prefix у- plus строить ("to build") — "to put together properly".
commonMistakes: устроить скандал is a figurative collocation meaning "to cause a scene".

synonymComparison.note: a more formal synonym for 'to organize,' used for larger-scale events.

past.n.gloss: Everything worked out as it should.

past.pl.gloss: We threw a celebration for the kids.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll throw a party on Saturday.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you organize the presentation?

imperative.sg.gloss: Arrange a meeting with him for me.

etymology: Derived from добрый ("good/kind"); the sense is "good/goodness".
commonMistakes: нет худа без добра is a standard proverb meaning "every cloud has a silver lining".

etymology: An adjectivized passive participle of любить ("to love").
commonMistakes: The nominalized use (любимый/любимая = "sweetheart") is also common — distinguish it from the adjective use.

etymology: An adjective derived from полиция ("police"), used as a noun.
commonMistakes: Since it's an adjective-origin noun, it declines like an adjective (hard-stem pattern).

etymology: Borrowed from Chinese chá, having entered Russian via the Silk Road.
commonMistakes: A partitive second genitive form чаю is sometimes used (выпить чаю).

etymology: The adverbial form of ужасный ("terrible").
commonMistakes: Frequently used colloquially as an intensifier meaning "very" (even in a positive sense).

aspectUsage: Imperfective for repeated/habitual buying; use the perfective купить for a single completed purchase.
etymology: Prefix по- plus the imperfective derivative of купить ("to buy").
commonMistakes: Mind the aspect pair покупать (buying, process/habit) versus купить (to complete a purchase).

examples.gloss: We buy groceries at the market.
She bought a dress for the wedding.

synonymComparison.note: a more formal synonym for 'to purchase, acquire.'

past.m.gloss: He used to buy groceries on the way.

past.f.gloss: She used to buy books regularly.

past.n.gloss: Everything used to sell fast at the sale.

past.pl.gloss: We used to buy tickets in advance.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you buy materials wholesale?

etymology: Prefix по- plus an archaic добный ("resembling").
commonMistakes: ничего подобного is a strong idiom meaning "nothing of the sort / no way".

etymology: Borrowed from German Stück ("a piece/item").
commonMistakes: Used colloquially as a catch-all word for "thing/business/situation" — mind the broad usage.

aspectUsage: A perfective related word meaning "to become necessary". нуждаться ("to need") takes a different subject structure — not a true aspectual pair.
etymology: Prefix по- plus an archaic надобиться ("to be necessary").
commonMistakes: Takes a dative experiencer (мне понадобится = "I will need [it]").

governance.pattern: dative (person who needs it) + nominative (thing needed)

synonymComparison.note: понадобиться ('to become necessary,' with the thing as subject) differs from нуждаться ('to need,' with the person as subject).

past.m.gloss: The passport was needed right away.

past.f.gloss: A certificate was needed for the visa.

past.n.gloss: A permit was needed at the entrance.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: You'll be needed at the meeting.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: (rare usage) We ourselves will be needed.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: (rare usage) You'll be needed at the presentation.

etymology: The adverbial form of совершенный ("perfect/complete").
commonMistakes: совершенно верно is a standard way to agree, "absolutely right".

aspectUsage: A perfective related word meaning "to go somewhere and come back (round trip)"; its corresponding imperfective is ходить (multidirectional).
etymology: Prefix с- plus ходить ("to walk") — "to go and return".
commonMistakes: сходить implies a completed round trip, unlike пойти (one-way).

governance.pattern: в/на + accusative (place of the round trip)

example.gloss: I went to the store (and back).

examples.gloss: She went to see the doctor.

synonymComparison.note: a close synonym for a round trip by vehicle; сходить implies the round trip is on foot.

past.m.gloss: He went to the post office and back.

past.f.gloss: She went to scout things out.

past.n.gloss: Everything used to go unpunished easily.

past.pl.gloss: We went to the movies yesterday.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you go to the pharmacy?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll go scout it out himself.

nonpast.1pl.ru: Мы сходим на выставку в субботу.
nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll go to the exhibition on Saturday.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you go to the post office today?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll go for a walk in the evening.

etymology: Derived from записать ("to write down").
commonMistakes: Covers both "recording" and "[appointment] booking/registration" — context decides which.

etymology: Negative prefix не- plus большой ("big") — "not very big".
commonMistakes: A somewhat softer/more modest way of saying "not very big" than маленький ("small").

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing process of dying; use the perfective умереть for a single completed death.
etymology: The imperfective derivative of умереть ("to die").
commonMistakes: умирать от скуки/смеха are figurative idioms meaning "to be bored to death / die laughing".

examples.gloss: The tradition is dying out over time.

synonymComparison.note: a synonym for a sudden death — in an accident, disaster, or war.

past.m.gloss: The forest was dying from drought.

past.n.gloss: Everything was dying out in this town.

past.pl.gloss: Old traditions were gradually dying out.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Aren't you starving?

nonpast.3pl.ru: Старые виды умирают один за другим.
nonpast.3pl.gloss: Old species are dying out one by one.

imperative.pl.gloss: Don't let the heat get to you.

etymology: Borrowed from French toilette, originally meaning "grooming/dressing".
commonMistakes: Because of its French origin, уборная can be used as a more polite alternative.

etymology: An old Russian word for a peasant man; in modern colloquial speech it now generally means "guy/bloke".
commonMistakes: A very casual slang word — use мужчина in formal contexts.

etymology: где ("where") plus the indefinite particle -то.
commonMistakes: Besides "somewhere", it's also used colloquially to mean "approximately" (где-то в пять часов = "around five o'clock").

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed glance; взглядывать (its imperfective) exists but is rare in use.
etymology: Prefix вз- ("upward") plus an archaic глянуть ("to look") — "to raise one's gaze".
commonMistakes: взглянуть denotes a single, brief glance — shorter than посмотреть.

examples.gloss: She looked at me with surprise.

examples.ru: Он время от времени взглядывает на дверь.
examples.gloss: He glances at the door from time to time.
She was nervously glancing at the clock.

synonymComparison.note: a close synonym differing in duration: взглянуть is a brief glance, посмотреть implies a longer look.

past.f.gloss: She looked up from under her brow.

past.n.gloss: The sun peeked out from behind the clouds (figurative).

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you glance at the report?

nonpast.1pl.gloss: Let's look at the problem differently.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Would you glance at the document?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll look at the proposal later.

etymology: Prefix о- plus a root related to громадный ("so big it makes noise").
commonMistakes: A stronger degree than большой — closer to "huge/enormous".

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of disappearing; use пропадать for repeated/ongoing disappearing.
etymology: Prefix про- plus an archaic пасть ("to fall") — "to fall away and vanish".
commonMistakes: пропасть без вести is a standard idiom meaning "to go missing without a trace".

governance.pattern: used with adverbs/context (to vanish/go missing, intransitive)

examples.gloss: The keys disappeared from the bag.

examples.ru: Он пропадает на работе целыми днями.
examples.gloss: He's buried in work all day long.

synonymComparison.note: nearly synonymous, but исчезнуть conveys a more instant, definitive disappearance.

past.pl.gloss: The documents went missing during the move.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: You'll fall off the radar if you don't call.

nonpast.2pl.ru: Вы не пропадёте в новом городе.
nonpast.2pl.gloss: You'll be fine in the new city.

etymology: Derived from зад ("rear/behind"); a vulgar/colloquial word.
commonMistakes: A fairly crude slang word — зад/попа are more appropriate in formal contexts.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of finding out/clarifying; use выяснять for repeated/ongoing investigation.
etymology: Prefix вы- plus ясный ("clear") — "to bring into the clear".
commonMistakes: выяснить отношения is a standard idiom meaning "to hash things out / clear the air".

examples.gloss: He found out the details in advance.
The police are investigating the circumstances.
We're figuring out the reasons for the refusal.

synonymComparison.note: выяснить ('to find out through investigation,' more active) differs from узнать ('to learn/find out,' more general).

past.m.gloss: He found out everything in detail.

past.n.gloss: Everything came to light by chance.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you find out the reason for the delay?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll clarify the details of the contract.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you determine the cause of the error?

etymology: Derived from угодить ("to please/suit"); the original sense is "in a pleasing way".
commonMistakes: Combined with a question word, угодно forms a generalizing "any-" meaning (кто угодно = "anyone at all").

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "acting / enrolling"; use поступать for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: Prefix по- plus an archaic ступить ("to step") — "to take a step".
commonMistakes: Covers both "to enroll [in university]" and "to act [in a certain way]" — context decides which.

examples.gloss: Money comes into the account regularly.

synonymComparison.note: a more general phrase for 'to behave,' focusing on character/attitude.

past.n.gloss: The application came in on time.

past.pl.gloss: We acted according to the rules.

nonpast.3sg.ru: Он поступит в институт в этом году.
nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll enroll in college this year.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you act according to the law?

imperative.sg.gloss: Do what you think is best.

etymology: Derived from дарить ("to give as a gift").
commonMistakes: Note the fleeting vowel that drops in declension (подарок→подарка).

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "calling/summoning"; use вызывать for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: Prefix вы- ("out") plus звать ("to call") — "to call out".
commonMistakes: вызвать интерес/подозрение is a figurative collocation meaning "to arouse interest/suspicion".

synonymComparison.note: позвать ('to call,' simpler, for a person) differs from вызвать ('to summon officially,' or 'to cause').

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you call security?

etymology: Prefix за- plus an archaic кон ("boundary/order") — "a set boundary/rule".
commonMistakes: Distinguish правило (an everyday rule) from закон (a state law).

etymology: A basic word tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to bite".
commonMistakes: вооружён до зубов is a figurative idiom meaning "armed to the teeth".

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of inviting; use приглашать for repeated/ongoing inviting.
etymology: Prefix при- plus an archaic гласить ("to call out").
commonMistakes: пригласить на танец is a standard collocation meaning "to ask [someone] to dance".

synonymComparison.note: пригласить ('to invite formally') differs from звать ('to call/invite,' more general/casual).

past.m.gloss: He invited partners to the meeting.

past.f.gloss: She invited the professor to speak.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll invite you to the wedding.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll invite the team to lunch.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll invite guests to the anniversary.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you invite us to the opening?

etymology: The adverbial form of честный ("honest").
commonMistakes: честно говоря is a frequent discourse marker meaning "honestly speaking".

etymology: A basic word tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "ear"; its plural уши is irregular.
commonMistakes: The plural уши and genitive ушей diverge substantially from the singular — an irregular paradigm.

etymology: как ("how") plus the indefinite particle -то.
commonMistakes: Mind both senses: как-то раз ("once/one time") and как-то ("somehow/vaguely").

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "limb/part".
commonMistakes: Carries both the "[organization] member" sense and a vulgar body-part euphemism — mind the context.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of winning; use выигрывать for repeated/ongoing winning.
etymology: Prefix вы- plus играть ("to play/compete") — "to win through competing".
commonMistakes: выиграть время is a figurative idiom meaning "to buy time".

examples.gloss: We save time by working together.

synonymComparison.note: a close synonym: выиграть is to win a prize/game, while победить is to defeat an opponent.

past.pl.gloss: We gained time thanks to the plan.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll win the case in court.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You'll win the prize.

etymology: Derived from простить ("to forgive").
commonMistakes: просить прощения is the essential standard phrase for "to apologize".

etymology: Borrowed from Greek mousike ("the art of the Muses").
commonMistakes: An uncountable collective noun, used only in the singular.

etymology: Derived from состоять ("to consist/be in a state").
commonMistakes: Besides "state/condition", it also keeps an older sense of "fortune/wealth" (человек с состоянием = "a man of means").

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of changing; use изменяться for repeated/ongoing change.
etymology: A reflexive derivative of изменить ("to change something") — "to change oneself".
commonMistakes: Don't confuse the intransitive измениться ("to change/become different") with the transitive изменить ("to change something").

synonymComparison.note: a synonym for a more dramatic transformation — 'to be transformed.'

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll change along with the market.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You'll change if you try.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root for the numeral "six".
commonMistakes: Like other numerals 5+, it's followed by the genitive plural (шесть часов).

etymology: Derived from грязь ("mud/dirt").
commonMistakes: грязная игра is a figurative phrase meaning "dirty tricks/underhanded play".

etymology: Derived from the root that gave советовать ("to advise"); the original sense is "consultation/advice".
commonMistakes: Carries both "advice" and the historical "[Soviet-era] council" sense — mind the context.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of running away. Note that the homonymous imperfective сбегать also has a separate sense: "to make a quick round trip".
etymology: Prefix с- ("away") plus бежать ("to run") — "to run away".
commonMistakes: Mind that сбегать (imperfective) has an entirely different meaning, "to quickly go there and back".

examples.gloss: The criminal fled from the police.
Kids rarely run away from home.

synonymComparison.note: nearly synonymous, but сбежать leans slightly more toward 'sneaking away, fleeing covertly.'

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Are you going to run off from work?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll escape at the first opportunity.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll run away from our problems.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you sneak out of the party early?

etymology: в plus an archaic нутро ("interior") — an adverb/preposition.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse внутри (static location "inside") with внутрь (direction "into/inward").

etymology: Derived from an archaic сватать ("to arrange a marriage").
commonMistakes: The genitive plural свадеб is regular, but its pattern is easy to forget.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of tidying/removing; use убирать for repeated/ongoing tidying.
etymology: Prefix у- ("away") plus брать ("to take") — "to take away".
commonMistakes: Убери руки! is also used as a sharp command, "Hands off!"

examples.gloss: He cleans the apartment every Saturday.

synonymComparison.note: a more specific synonym for 'to clean/scrub' (polishing, scrubbing).

past.f.gloss: She put her things away in the closet.

past.n.gloss: Everything got cleaned up in an hour.

past.pl.gloss: We cleaned the yard before the holiday.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll have everything cleaned up by evening.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you clean up the grounds?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll clear the snow by morning.

imperative.pl.gloss: Clean the room before the guests arrive.

etymology: Borrowed from English "boss", ultimately from Dutch baas ("master").
commonMistakes: Distinguish начальник (the more formal "boss/supervisor") from the more colloquial босс.

aspectUsage: A multidirectional, habitual imperfective ("to carry/wear") with no true perfective counterpart (отнести/принести etc. are used depending on context).
etymology: The multidirectional form of нести ("to carry [one way]").
commonMistakes: Distinguish носить (habitual/multidirectional) from нести (a single directed act of carrying).

examples.gloss: He wears a uniform at work.
I carry a backpack every day.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: носить is the habitual/multidirectional 'to wear/carry,' while нести is the single-direction 'to be carrying right now.'

past.m.gloss: He used to wear a suit every day.

past.f.gloss: She used to have long hair.

past.n.gloss: Everything bore the marks of time.

past.pl.gloss: We used to wear uniforms at school.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I wear a ring as a keepsake.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you wear a mask at work?

etymology: A basic word tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "sea".
commonMistakes: Also note the figurative construction море + genitive (море вопросов = "a sea of questions").

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of tying/connecting; use связывать for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: Prefix с- plus вязать ("to knit/tie").
commonMistakes: Covers both "to tie up (with rope)" and "to knit" — context decides which.

examples.gloss: She knitted a scarf for her grandmother.
Friendship has bound them together for years.
I associate success with hard work.

synonymComparison.note: a more physical/technical synonym for 'to connect/join.'

past.m.ru: Он связал свою судьбу с компанией.
past.m.gloss: He tied his fate to the company.

past.f.gloss: She devoted her life to music.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll connect you with the manager.

nonpast.2pl.ru: Вы свяжете меня с отделом продаж?
nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you connect me with the sales department?

imperative.sg.gloss: Tie the ends of the rope together.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of starting; use начинаться for the ongoing process of beginning.
etymology: A reflexive derivative of начать ("to start something") — "to start by itself".
commonMistakes: Don't confuse the intransitive начаться ("to begin [by itself]") with the transitive начать ("to start something").

examples.gloss: The movie starts with the credits.

synonymComparison.note: a more colloquial, English-derived synonym for 'to kick off' (sports, events).

nonpast.1sg.ru: Я начнусь с начала, если смогу.
nonpast.1sg.gloss: (rare usage) I will start over from the beginning, if I can.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: (rare usage) You will start anew whenever you want.

nonpast.1pl.ru: Мы начнёмся вовремя, если всё готово.
nonpast.1pl.gloss: (rare usage) We will start on time, if everything is ready.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: (rare usage) You all will start with a slight delay.

nonpast.3pl.gloss: The competition will start at noon.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of destroying; use уничтожать for repeated/ongoing destruction.
etymology: Prefix у- ("completely") plus ничто ("nothing") — "to reduce to nothing".
commonMistakes: уничтожить улики/документы is a standard collocation meaning "to dispose of evidence/documents".

examples.gloss: The company disposes of waste safely.

synonymComparison.note: a close synonym for 'to destroy,' but разрушить focuses more on physical collapse of structures.

past.f.gloss: The disease wiped out the harvest.

past.n.gloss: Everything was destroyed by the war.

past.pl.gloss: We disposed of the old documents.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Are you going to destroy the evidence?

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you dispose of these samples?

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of informing; use сообщать for repeated/ongoing informing.
etymology: Prefix со- plus общий ("common/shared") — "to share → to inform".
commonMistakes: The common construction is сообщить + dative + о + prepositional (сообщить ему о проблеме).

example.gloss: He told me about the meeting.

examples.gloss: We reported the results on time.
The press reports on the event daily.

synonymComparison.note: a more formal/business-like synonym for 'to inform.'

past.pl.gloss: We informed clients about the delay.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll let you know the result.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you tell me about the decision?

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll notify you of changes in advance.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you let us know when you arrive?

aspectUsage: Imperfective for repeated/habitual sitting down; use the perfective сесть for a single completed act.
etymology: The imperfective derivative of сесть ("to sit down"), from an archaic root сед- ("to sit").
commonMistakes: Don't confuse садиться (the act of sitting down) with сидеть (the state of sitting).

example.gloss: He's sitting down on the chair.

examples.ru: Она садится за стол каждый вечер в семь.
examples.gloss: She sits down at the table at seven every evening.
The sun is setting below the horizon.
He sat down next to me.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: садиться (a different root) is the action of sitting down, while сидеть is the resulting state of being seated.

past.m.gloss: He used to sit down last.

past.f.gloss: She used to sit by the window.

past.pl.gloss: We used to sit down at the table together.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Are you getting behind the wheel?

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Are you sitting in the front row?

etymology: The adverbial form of далёкий ("distant").
commonMistakes: Don't confuse the adverb далеко with the adjective далёкий.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of sitting down; use садиться for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: A basic verb from an archaic root сед- ("to sit").
commonMistakes: Note the figurative collocations сесть в тюрьму ("to go to prison") and сесть за руль ("to get behind the wheel / start driving").

example.gloss: I sat down on the bench.

examples.gloss: He sat down at the computer.

examples.ru: Он садится рано утром за работу.
examples.gloss: He sits down to work early in the morning.
The sun sets late in summer.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: сесть (perfective) is the action of sitting down, while сидеть (a different root) is the resulting state of being seated.

past.f.gloss: She sat down across from him.

past.n.gloss: The sun set behind the clouds.

past.pl.gloss: We sat down to dinner together.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you sit next to me?

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you sit down at the negotiating table?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll sit in the front row.

etymology: во plus круг ("circle") — "around".
commonMistakes: Takes вокруг + genitive (вокруг стола = "around the table").

etymology: Borrowed via German Küche, ultimately from Latin coquina ("kitchen").
commonMistakes: Besides "kitchen", it also means "cuisine/cooking style" (домашняя кухня = "home cooking").

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of coming up with/inventing; use придумывать for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: Prefix при- plus думать ("to think") — "to think up".
commonMistakes: Distinguish придумать (to invent, neutral/positive) from выдумать (to make up a falsehood, often negative).

example.gloss: He came up with a plan.

examples.gloss: She came up with a great idea.
We came up with a name.
He's always coming up with excuses.
Kids invent games on their own.

synonymComparison.note: a more technical synonym for 'to invent' (an innovation).

past.f.gloss: She came up with a joke.

past.n.gloss: It all came together on its own.

past.pl.gloss: We came up with a new system.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you come up with an excuse?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll come up with a solution.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you come up with a brand name?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll come up with a new product.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "one who sits nearby".
commonMistakes: Mind the irregular plural соседи, not the expected *соседы.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of proposing/offering; use предлагать for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: Prefix пред- plus an archaic ложить ("to place") — "to put forward".
commonMistakes: предложить руку и сердце is a standard idiom meaning "to propose marriage".

synonymComparison.note: советовать ('to advise') differs from предложить ('to propose/offer') — giving an opinion vs. offering an option.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll propose an option to you.

nonpast.2sg.ru: Ты предложишь ей руку и сердце?

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you propose the terms?

etymology: Borrowed from French pistolet, likely from an old Czech firearm name.
commonMistakes: Distinguish ружьё (a rifle/shotgun) from пистолет (a handgun) by size and type.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "big"; in older Russian it already carried the sense "great".
commonMistakes: Distinguish большой (merely big) from великий (great, qualitatively outstanding).

etymology: Derived from малый ("small"); an affectionate diminutive meaning "little one".
commonMistakes: Has an affectionate tone — use ребёнок in formal contexts.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for repeated/habitual dropping by/entering; use the perfective зайти for a single completed instance.
etymology: The imperfective derivative of зайти.
commonMistakes: заходить на сайт is a modern figurative expression meaning "to visit a website".

example.ru: Он заходит в кафе каждый день.
example.gloss: He stops by the café every day.

examples.ru: Она заходит в гости по субботам.

examples.gloss: He stopped by for a minute.
The sun set behind the mountains.

synonymComparison.note: a close synonym: заходить focuses on dropping in/entering, while уходить means leaving a place altogether.

past.f.gloss: She used to stop by to check the mail.

past.n.gloss: Everything was going according to plan.

past.pl.ru: Мы заходили в гости по очереди.
past.pl.gloss: We used to visit each other in turn.

nonpast.1sg.ru: Я захожу на сайт каждый день.
nonpast.1sg.gloss: I visit the site every day.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He logs into the app regularly.

nonpast.1pl.ru: Мы заходим в систему через пароль.
nonpast.1pl.gloss: We log into the system with a password.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you stop by the store often?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They rarely come by our place.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of agreeing; use соглашаться for repeated/ongoing agreeing.
etymology: Prefix со- plus an archaic гласить ("to say") — "to voice together → to agree".
commonMistakes: Takes согласиться с + instrumental (согласиться с мнением).

examples.gloss: He always agrees with his boss.

examples.ru: Мы редко соглашаемся по этому вопросу.
examples.gloss: We rarely agree on this issue.

synonymComparison.note: a more official synonym for 'to approve.'

past.n.gloss: The board agreed to the changes.

past.pl.gloss: We agreed to the terms of the contract.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you agree to these terms?

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you agree to revise the terms?

etymology: Derived from the root of повести ("to lead"); the original sense is "a lead rein / reason".
commonMistakes: по поводу is a standard fixed preposition phrase meaning "regarding".

etymology: A determiner related to весь ("all"); the original sense is "any/every kind of".
commonMistakes: на всякий случай is the essential standard phrase meaning "just in case".

etymology: Derived from удаться ("to succeed/turn out well").
commonMistakes: Желаю удачи! is the standard phrase for "good luck!"

etymology: A basic word tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "fire", with a fleeting vowel (огонь→огня).
commonMistakes: играть с огнём is a figurative idiom meaning "to play with fire / take a risk".

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of meeting/greeting; use встречать for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: Derived from the root of встреча ("encounter").
commonMistakes: встретить Новый год is a standard idiom meaning "to see in the New Year".

examples.gloss: He ran into her by chance.
We met the guests at the airport.

examples.ru: Он встречает Новый год с семьёй.
examples.gloss: He celebrates New Year with his family.
We greet clients at the entrance.

synonymComparison.note: встретить ('to meet/encounter,' works for both known and new people) differs from познакомиться ('to meet for the first time').

past.m.gloss: He ran into an old friend.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll meet you at the station.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll greet the dawn on the beach.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you meet us at the airport?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll meet the team at the entrance.

etymology: Derived from an archaic речь ("to say"); the sense is "speech/words".
commonMistakes: часть речи is the standard grammatical term for "part of speech".

etymology: A basic word tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "hair"; the singular is rarely used, the plural волосы being standard.
commonMistakes: The singular волос is rarely used; the plural волосы (hair as a whole) is the normal everyday form.

etymology: From Greek phos ("light") plus graphein ("to draw") — "drawing with light".
commonMistakes: Both the clipped indeclinable фото and the full declinable фотография are used.

etymology: не plus уже plus an archaic question particle ли — an interrogative particle expressing strong surprise.
commonMistakes: Nearly synonymous with разве, but неужели carries stronger surprise/shock.

etymology: о- plus an archaic очи ("eyes") plus видный ("visible") — "visible to the eye, evident".
commonMistakes: The neuter short form очевидно is also very commonly used as a sentence-initial adverb ("obviously").

etymology: The adverbial form of крутой ("steep"), which developed a colloquial sense of "awesome/cool".
commonMistakes: Distinguish the literal "steep" sense from the colloquial "cool" sense by context.

etymology: Derived from ум ("intellect").
commonMistakes: Distinguish умный (intellectually smart) from мудрый (wise through experience).

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing an ongoing state of missing/being bored. соскучиться is a related word meaning "to start missing increasingly" — not a true aspectual pair.
etymology: Derived from скука ("boredom").
commonMistakes: Takes скучать по + dative (скучать по тебе, not "скучать тебя").

examples.gloss: The kids get bored/lonely without friends.

synonymComparison.note: a stronger synonym for 'to yearn/long for,' with more emotional intensity.

past.m.gloss: He was homesick for his homeland.

past.pl.gloss: We were homesick for a long time.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you miss your old job?

imperative.pl.gloss: Don't be lonely, we'll be back soon.

etymology: Prefix в- plus an archaic друг ("suddenly", unrelated to the modern word for "friend").
commonMistakes: а вдруг is a colloquial phrase expressing a hypothetical worry, "what if".

etymology: From Old Church Slavonic красьнъ ("beautiful"); the modern word narrowed to mean specifically "red".
commonMistakes: Note that "Red Square" (Красная площадь) owes its name to the old meaning "beautiful", not the color.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for habitual/ongoing lying; use the perfective соврать for a single completed lie.
etymology: A colloquial verb, possibly tracing to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to speak".
commonMistakes: Distinguish лгать (literary "to lie") from врать (the frequent colloquial synonym) by register.

examples.gloss: He lies without a shred of guilt.
She lied so as not to hurt someone.

synonymComparison.note: nearly synonymous, but лгать is more literary/formal; врать is the colloquial choice.

past.n.gloss: Everything in this story was a lie.

past.pl.gloss: We were lying for a joke.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Are you lying to me right now?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He lies as easily as breathing (fixed saying).

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We don't lie to each other.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Are you lying intentionally?

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed attempt; use пытаться for repeated/ongoing attempting.
etymology: A reflexive derivative of an archaic пытать ("to test").
commonMistakes: Takes попытаться + infinitive (попытаться помочь).

examples.gloss: We tried to come to an agreement.
He keeps trying to improve the result.
We're trying to find a solution.

synonymComparison.note: попытаться ('to attempt/make an effort') and попробовать ('to try/taste something') are similar but differ in what they apply to.

past.n.gloss: Everything tried to come together successfully.

past.pl.gloss: We tried to find a compromise.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll try to fix the mistake.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll try to make it on time.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you try to get in touch with him?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll try to settle the dispute.

etymology: Derived from гореть ("to burn").
commonMistakes: горячая тема/новость is a figurative phrase meaning "a hot topic".

etymology: Derived from a root related to an archaic стеречь ("to watch over/guard").
commonMistakes: The short forms осторожен/осторожна/осторожно are often used in the warning будь осторожен! ("be careful!").

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing the ongoing state of being ill; use the perfective заболеть for a single completed onset of illness.
etymology: Derived from боль ("pain").
commonMistakes: A homonymous 3rd-person-only form болит ("[it] hurts") follows a completely different conjugation pattern — don't confuse it with this verb (a person being ill).

examples.gloss: She gets sick often in winter.
I'm rooting for this team (a different sense).
She came down with the flu.

synonymComparison.note: a more colloquial/old-fashioned synonym for 'to be sick.'

past.m.gloss: He was sick for a long time.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Which team do you root for?

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We get sick together every winter.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you root for the national team?

etymology: Borrowed from Greek idiotes ("a private/unskilled person"), which developed into an insult.
commonMistakes: A fairly harsh insult — avoid it outside casual joking among friends.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed impersonal event of "being lucky" (dative construction). The corresponding imperfective везти has the same form but a separate "to transport" meaning.
etymology: Prefix по- plus везти ("to carry/transport") — the sense developed to "luck being brought to someone".
commonMistakes: Mostly used only in the 3rd-person singular impersonal (повезло/повезёт), taking a dative experiencer (тебе повезло = "you got lucky").

example.gloss: I was lucky enough to find a job.

examples.gloss: We got lucky with the weather.
She was lucky to meet him.

synonymComparison.note: повезти ('to be lucky,' emphasizing chance) differs from удаться ('to succeed/work out,' emphasizing the outcome).

past.m.gloss: He got lucky at the last moment.

past.f.gloss: (transportation sense) The car drove us to the airport.

past.pl.gloss: (transportation sense) They transported the goods to the market.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: (transportation sense) Will you drive us to the station?

nonpast.1pl.gloss: (transportation sense) We'll take the guests on a tour.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: (transportation sense) Will you drive the kids to school?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: (transportation sense) The cargo will be delivered to them tomorrow.

imperative.sg.gloss: (transportation sense) Drive me to the station.

etymology: An affectionate diminutive of минута ("minute").
commonMistakes: Минутку! is a standard everyday phrase meaning "Just a moment!"

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of "approaching/suiting"; use the perfective подойти for a single completed instance.
etymology: The imperfective derivative of подойти.
commonMistakes: Covers both "to come closer" and "to fit/suit [in size, etc.]" — context decides which.

examples.gloss: He's nearing the end of his work.

synonymComparison.note: a more formal synonym for 'to draw near/approach' physically.

past.n.gloss: Everything was coming to a close.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'm nearing the end of the chapter.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Are you getting close to a solution?

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We're approaching the final stage of the project.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Are you getting closer to understanding the problem?

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "high".
commonMistakes: The short forms высок/высока/высоко are used in predicate position.

etymology: Borrowed from English "show"; an indeclinable neuter noun.
commonMistakes: As a loanword, its form stays the same across all cases.

etymology: A lexicalized neuter short form of больной ("painful"), used as an impersonal predicate.
commonMistakes: Takes больно + dative (мне больно = "it hurts me").

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of vanishing; use исчезать for repeated/ongoing disappearing.
etymology: Prefix ис- ("out") plus an archaic чезнуть ("to vanish").
commonMistakes: The masculine past form исчез drops the -ну- suffix rather than becoming *исчезнул.

examples.gloss: The problem disappeared on its own.
The money disappeared from the account.

examples.ru: Он исчезает на несколько дней регулярно.
examples.gloss: He regularly disappears for a few days.

synonymComparison.note: nearly synonymous, but исчезнуть conveys a more instant, definitive disappearance; пропасть is more colloquial.

past.f.gloss: The pain disappeared after the medicine.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: The problem will go away on its own.

nonpast.1pl.ru: Мы исчезнем с радаров на неделю.
nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll be off the grid for a week (figurative).

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you vanish without a trace?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll disappear at the first sign of threat.

etymology: The adverbial form of трудный ("difficult").
commonMistakes: Note the impersonal construction трудно + dative (мне трудно = "it's hard for me").

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of creating; use создавать for repeated/ongoing creating.
etymology: Prefix со- ("together") plus an archaic здать ("to form").
commonMistakes: создать впечатление is a figurative collocation meaning "to create an impression".

examples.gloss: She created a work of art.
He's been creating music for years.

synonymComparison.note: a more institutional synonym for 'to found/establish' (an organization).

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you create a separate group?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll create a new product line.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root shared by "right (correct)" and "right (direction)".
commonMistakes: Distinguish правый (the adjective "right [side]") from the similar-looking short form прав ("[you are] correct") — separate words.

etymology: Derived from предложить ("to propose"); also used as the grammar term "sentence".
commonMistakes: Covers both "proposal" and the grammatical "sentence" — context decides which.

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing the ongoing state of "existing", with no true perfective counterpart (просуществовать is a related word meaning "to exist for a period of time").
etymology: Prefix су- ("together") plus an archaic щество ("essence").
commonMistakes: существовать is an abstract "to exist" — don't confuse it with жить ("to live", more concrete).

examples.gloss: This tradition has existed for centuries.

synonymComparison.note: существовать ('to exist,' more formal) is close to быть ('to be,' more general), but существовать emphasizes abstract/ongoing existence.

past.m.gloss: The city existed for a thousand years.

past.f.gloss: The legend existed long before us.

past.n.gloss: The state existed for only a short time.

nonpast.2sg.ru: Ты существуешь только в моих мыслях.
nonpast.2sg.gloss: You exist only in my thoughts.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: The problem has existed for a long time.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you exist independently?

etymology: Derived from боль ("pain").
commonMistakes: Distinguish боль (pain itself) from болезнь (the state of being ill).

etymology: An adjectivized past participle of быть ("to be"); the original sense is "having formerly been".
commonMistakes: The nominalized use (бывший/бывшая = "ex [partner]") is also common — distinguish it from the adjective use.

etymology: A kinship term for "uncle", likely of nursery-word origin; grammatically ends in -я but is masculine.
commonMistakes: A masculine noun that declines like a feminine -я noun (дядя, дяди, дяде...).

etymology: The adverbial form of постоянный ("constant").
commonMistakes: Distinguish всегда (always, absolute) from постоянно (constantly/repeatedly, with a slightly colloquial, often complaining nuance).

etymology: The suppletive superlative form of хороший ("good").
commonMistakes: Distinguish лучше (the comparative adverb/adjective) from лучший (the superlative adjective).

etymology: на plus an archaic пример ("example") — an adverb/discourse marker.
commonMistakes: A frequent sentence-initial/medial discourse marker — note it's set off by commas.

etymology: Derived from знать ("to know"); also nominalized to mean "an acquaintance".
commonMistakes: Covers both the nominalized "acquaintance" and the adjective use (знакомое лицо = "a familiar face") — context decides which.

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing an ongoing state of suspicion; use the perfective заподозрить for a single completed onset of suspicion.
etymology: Prefix по- plus an archaic дозирать ("to look [at]") — "to look behind → to suspect".
commonMistakes: Takes подозревать + accusative + в + prepositional (подозревать его в обмане = "to suspect him of deceit").

example.gloss: The police suspect him of theft.

examples.gloss: She suspects her husband of cheating.
He immediately suspected something was wrong.

synonymComparison.note: подозревать ('to suspect,' a specific accusation) differs from сомневаться ('to doubt,' a more general uncertainty).

past.f.gloss: She had suspected something wrong for a long time.

past.n.gloss: Everything had been suspected from the very start.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you suspect a violation?

etymology: A collective noun derived from родить ("to give birth"); the original sense is "those who were born [here]".
commonMistakes: The partitive form народу is used colloquially to express quantity.

etymology: An affectionate diminutive of an archaic дед ("grandfather").
commonMistakes: A masculine noun that declines like a feminine -а noun.

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing an ongoing state of "expecting/waiting", with no true perfective counterpart.
etymology: Prefix о- plus an archaic жидать ("to wait").
commonMistakes: More literary/formal in tone than the everyday ждать ("to wait").

examples.gloss: We're expecting guests in the evening.

synonymComparison.note: ожидать ('to expect/anticipate,' more formal) is close to ждать ('to wait,' more general/colloquial).

past.f.gloss: She waited for a call all day.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We're awaiting the arrival of the cargo.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Are you expecting support from investors?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They're expecting the project to be completed.

imperative.sg.gloss: Wait for me at the entrance.

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing an ongoing state of wishing/desiring; use the perfective пожелать for a single completed expression of a wish.
etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to desire".
commonMistakes: оставляет желать лучшего is a standard euphemism meaning "leaves something to be desired".

synonymComparison.note: желать ('to wish,' more formal, for others' well-being) differs from хотеть ('to want,' one's own desire).

past.m.gloss: He wished her nothing but good.

past.f.gloss: She had wished for change for a long time.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I wish you all the best.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He wishes for a better life.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you wish to continue?

etymology: Borrowed from Latin charta ("paper"); polysemous for "map", "[playing] card", and "[credit] card".
commonMistakes: Carries several meanings — "map", "card", "playing card" — mind the context.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to follow/track".
commonMistakes: оставить след is also used figuratively, meaning "to leave a [lasting] mark".

etymology: Derived from an archaic обычать ("to accustom").
commonMistakes: Note the contrast between обычный (ordinary) and особый (special).

etymology: Borrowed from French autobus — auto ("self") plus (omni)bus ("for everyone").
commonMistakes: "By bus" is на автобусе (prepositional + preposition на).

etymology: Borrowed from French sérieux, ultimately from Latin serius ("grave/weighty").
commonMistakes: The short forms серьёзен/серьёзна/серьёзно are used in predicate position.

etymology: An ordinal numeral developed from the Proto-Indo-European "three" series.
commonMistakes: An irregular soft-stem ordinal with special endings (третья, третье) — mind the pattern.

aspectUsage: In the copular sense "to be", a stative use with no perfective counterpart.
etymology: The imperfective derivative of явиться ("to appear"), which came to serve as a formal written substitute for быть.
commonMistakes: A formal, written-register expression — быть is more natural in speech.

examples.ru: Она является экспертом в этой области.
examples.gloss: She is an expert in this field.

synonymComparison.note: являться ('to be,' more formal/written) is nearly synonymous with быть ('to be,' more general/colloquial) but differs in register.

past.m.gloss: He was the founder of the company.

past.f.gloss: She was a witness to the events.

past.pl.gloss: They were partners for a long time.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I am a representative of the company.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: You are part of the team.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He is the author of the book.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We are leaders in the industry.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You are a customer of our company.

etymology: Derived from край ("edge").
commonMistakes: в крайнем случае is a standard idiom meaning "as a last resort / worst case".

etymology: Derived from вина ("guilt/fault").
commonMistakes: Distinguish виновный (legally guilty) from виноватый (at fault/feeling guilty in everyday terms) by register.

aspectUsage: Imperfective expressing an ongoing state of "meaning", with no true perfective counterpart.
etymology: Prefix о- plus знак ("sign") — "to mark → to mean".
commonMistakes: Nearly synonymous with значить, but означать carries a more literary/formal tone.

synonymComparison.note: nearly synonymous, but значить is a more colloquial synonym for 'to mean.'

past.n.ru: Всё означало одно и то же.

nonpast.1sg.ru: Я ничего не означаю для них.
nonpast.1sg.gloss: I don't mean anything to them.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: You mean a lot to me.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We represent stability for our clients.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You mean hope for many.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of selling; use продавать for repeated/habitual selling.
etymology: Prefix про- plus дать ("to give") — "to give over, to sell".
commonMistakes: Mind the aspect pair продать (completed sale) versus продавать (ongoing process of selling).

example.gloss: He sold the house to his neighbor.

examples.gloss: She sold the painting to a collector.
We sold the entire batch of goods.
He sells furniture at the market.

synonymComparison.note: a more business/economic synonym for 'to sell off' (goods).

past.m.gloss: He sold the car at a good price.

past.f.gloss: She sold her shares in the company.

past.pl.gloss: We sold the tickets in advance.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Are you going to sell the apartment?

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll sell the remainder at a discount.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you sell the rights to the book?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll sell their shares on the market.

etymology: The adverbial form of частый ("frequent").
commonMistakes: Don't confuse частый (the adjective "frequent") with часто (the adverb "often").

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root for the numeral "ten".
commonMistakes: Like other numerals 5+, it's followed by the genitive plural (десять минут).

etymology: The adverbial form of милый ("cute/dear").
commonMistakes: Also used alone as an exclamation ("how cute").

etymology: какой ("what kind of") plus the indefinite particle -нибудь.
commonMistakes: Distinguish какой-то (a specific but unnamed one, known to the speaker) from какой-нибудь (any at all, unspecified).

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of getting up/standing; use вставать for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: A basic verb from an archaic root ста- ("to stand").
commonMistakes: встать на ноги is a figurative idiom meaning "to get back on one's feet / become independent".

governance.pattern: with adverbs/place phrases (to get up/stand, intransitive)

examples.gloss: He stood up to defend his friend.

examples.ru: Он встаёт в шесть каждый день.
examples.gloss: He gets up at six every day.
We get up to the alarm.

synonymComparison.note: a close synonym meaning 'to rise/get up,' with a broader range of use.

past.pl.gloss: We stood up at the same time.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll get up in a minute.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you get up a bit earlier?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll get back on his feet again.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you take my side?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll stand up for their rights.

etymology: Borrowed via Latin from Greek kentron ("center point").
commonMistakes: Covers both "downtown" and "[a facility's] center" — context decides which.

aspectUsage: A biaspectual verb (same form for both aspects), though modern Russian also uses a dedicated imperfective арестовывать.
etymology: Borrowed from French arrêter ("to stop"), narrowed to mean "to arrest".
commonMistakes: As an animate noun's object, note the accusative=genitive rule (арестовать подозреваемого).

examples.gloss: They regularly arrest criminals (using the imperfective арестовывать).

synonymComparison.note: a milder synonym for 'to detain' temporarily, before a formal arrest.

past.f.gloss: The police arrested a group of scammers.

past.n.gloss: The property was seized by the court.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you arrest him without a warrant?

nonpast.3sg.gloss: The court will freeze the company's accounts.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you arrest the suspect today?

etymology: The adverbial form of полный ("full").
commonMistakes: полностью согласен is a standard phrase meaning "I completely agree".

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of trying/making an effort; use the perfective постараться for a single completed attempt.
etymology: Derived from старый ("old", archaically also "experienced").
commonMistakes: Distinguish стараться (making an effort) from пытаться (attempting, regardless of effort level).

examples.gloss: He's trying with all his might.
He made an effort and succeeded.
I'll try to come on time.

synonymComparison.note: стараться ('to try hard, make an effort') differs from пытаться ('to attempt') in the sustained, diligent nuance.

past.m.gloss: He tried not to be late.

past.n.gloss: Everything was trying to come together well.

past.pl.gloss: We were trying to change the situation.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He's trying to make an impression.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You're making an effort in vain.

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They're trying to live up to the trust placed in them.

etymology: Borrowed from English "lady"; an indeclinable feminine noun.
commonMistakes: As a loanword, its form stays the same across all cases.

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of grabbing, or the impersonal state of "being enough"; use the perfective хватить for a single completed grab or sufficiency.
etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to take".
commonMistakes: Covers both "to grab" and the impersonal "to be enough/suffice" — context decides which.

examples.gloss: There aren't enough resources for the project.

synonymComparison.note: хватать ('to grab,' or the impersonal 'to be enough') differs in meaning from доставать ('to fetch/get out'); watch for this verb's dual senses.

past.n.gloss: There was no patience left at all.

past.pl.gloss: (rare usage) There wasn't enough money for rent.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I seize luck by the tail (fixed saying).

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you have enough resources?

etymology: Borrowed from French résultat, ultimately from Latin resultare ("to spring back").
commonMistakes: в результате is a standard connective phrase meaning "as a result".

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of recalling; use вспоминать for repeated/ongoing recollection.
etymology: Prefix вс- plus помнить ("to remember") — "to rise up in memory".
commonMistakes: Don't confuse вспомнить (the moment of recalling) with помнить (the ongoing state of remembering).

examples.gloss: He often reminisces about the past.

examples.ru: Мы вспоминаем те дни с улыбкой.
examples.gloss: We remember those days with a smile.

synonymComparison.note: an important contrast: вспомнить is the inchoative 'to recall, to come to remember,' while помнить is the stative 'to remember.'

past.n.gloss: Everything suddenly came back to mind.

past.pl.ru: Мы вспомнили этот случай с юмором.
past.pl.gloss: We recalled that incident with humor.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll recall the details in time.

nonpast.1pl.ru: Мы вспомним об этом с благодарностью.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you remember where you left your keys?

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of closing; use закрывать for repeated/ongoing closing.
etymology: Prefix за- plus an archaic крыть ("to cover") — "to cover and shut".
commonMistakes: закрыть вопрос is a figurative expression meaning "to settle/close out an issue".

examples.gloss: The bank closes inactive customers' accounts.
He turns a blind eye to problems.

synonymComparison.note: an important antonym: закрыть ('to close') is the opposite of открыть ('to open').

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll wrap up the project by Friday.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you close the shop early?

etymology: The comparative-origin derivative of старый ("old"); the sense is "elder/senior".
commonMistakes: Distinguish старый (simply old/aged) from старший (older than someone, inherently comparative).

etymology: Derived from an archaic здравие ("health").
commonMistakes: Будь здоров! is a set phrase meaning "bless you" (after a sneeze) or "take care".

etymology: Negative prefix не- plus плохо ("badly") — "not badly → fairly well".
commonMistakes: Though it looks like a double negative, it expresses a modest positive assessment ("pretty good").

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed death (e.g. accident/war); use погибать for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: Prefix по- plus an archaic гибнуть ("to perish").
commonMistakes: Distinguish умереть (dying in general) from погибнуть (dying violently/unnaturally, e.g. accident, war) by nuance.

examples.gloss: The harvest was destroyed by the drought.
Animal species are dying out from poaching.
Forests are being lost to fires.

synonymComparison.note: a contrast: погибнуть implies a sudden death (accident, disaster, war), while умереть is the general verb 'to die' (illness, etc. included).

past.f.gloss: The village was destroyed by fire.

past.n.gloss: Everything was lost in one night.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: You won't be ruined if you try hard (figurative).

nonpast.3sg.gloss: The project will fail without funding.

nonpast.1pl.ru: Мы не погибнем без плана Б.
nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll manage without a plan B.

nonpast.2pl.ru: Вы не погибнете от такой нагрузки.
nonpast.2pl.gloss: That workload won't do you in.

nonpast.3pl.gloss: The plants will die without water.

imperative.pl.gloss: Don't let this storm be the death of you.

etymology: Borrowed from English "club".
commonMistakes: Covers both "nightclub" and "[hobby/sports] club" — context decides which.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to sense slightly".
commonMistakes: чуть не is a standard construction meaning "almost [did something but didn't]".

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to breathe"; related to дышать (to breathe).
commonMistakes: The plural духи means something entirely different — "perfume" — not "spirits".

etymology: Negative prefix не- plus возможно ("possibly") — an impersonal predicate.
commonMistakes: Distinguish невозможно (impossible) from нельзя (forbidden/not allowed).

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed instance of becoming tired; use уставать for the ongoing process of tiring.
etymology: Prefix у- plus an archaic стать ("to become") — "to become tired".
commonMistakes: The imperative устань! is semantically odd (you can't command tiredness) and essentially never used in practice.

examples.gloss: She got tired after the hike.

examples.ru: Я никогда не устаю от этой музыки.
examples.gloss: I never get tired of this music.

synonymComparison.note: a more formal synonym for 'to become exhausted,' implying stronger fatigue.

past.n.gloss: Everything felt worn out by the end of the day (figurative).

past.pl.gloss: We were tired from the trip.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: You'll get tired of this noise.

nonpast.3sg.ru: Он устанет повторять одно и то же.
nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll get tired of repeating the same thing.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll get tired earlier than usual.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: You'll be tired from the flight.

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll get tired of waiting for an answer.

imperative.sg.gloss: Don't wear yourself out too soon.

imperative.pl.gloss: Don't exhaust yourselves in one day.

etymology: Derived from понять ("to understand"); the philosophical/logical term for "concept".
commonMistakes: не иметь понятия is a standard colloquial phrase meaning "to have no idea".

etymology: A lexicalized plural imperative of слушать ("to listen"), used as an attention-getting interjection.
commonMistakes: Although grammatically an imperative, it's used independently to open a statement and get attention.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "long [in time]".
commonMistakes: Distinguish долгий (long in time) from длинный (long in space).

etymology: Related to спешить ("to hurry"); the sense is "fast / coming soon".
commonMistakes: скорая помощь is a standard nominalized phrase meaning "ambulance".

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of "taking care of"; use заботиться for repeated/ongoing care.
etymology: Prefix по- plus заботиться ("to take care of").
commonMistakes: Takes позаботиться о + prepositional (позаботиться о себе = "to take care of oneself").

example.gloss: He took care of the details.

examples.gloss: She took care of the guests.
He takes care of his family.
We constantly take care of our clients.

synonymComparison.note: a more specific synonym for 'to tend/care for' (physical caregiving).

past.m.gloss: He took care of everything in advance.

past.f.gloss: She took care of the paperwork.

past.pl.gloss: We took care of the transportation.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Will you take care of this?

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll take care of the clients.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you take care of the tickets?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll take care of the guests.

etymology: A colloquial nickname for Saint Petersburg, deriving from the city's founder, Peter the Great (Пётр).
commonMistakes: Use Санкт-Петербург in formal contexts — Питер is strictly colloquial.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of refusing; use отказываться for repeated/ongoing refusal.
etymology: Prefix от- plus an archaic казать ("to show") in reflexive form — "to turn away from showing → refuse".
commonMistakes: Takes отказаться от + genitive (отказаться от предложения).

examples.gloss: The company is moving away from old methods.

synonymComparison.note: a more formal/official synonym for 'to reject' (a proposal, application).

past.n.gloss: Everything seemed to refuse to acknowledge the obvious (figurative).

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll back out of the deal.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you withdraw the lawsuit?

etymology: Borrowed from Latin secretus ("set apart, hidden").
commonMistakes: Distinguish секрет (a personal secret) from тайна (a deeper, more significant mystery).

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of missing/letting through; use пропускать for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: Prefix про- plus пустить ("to let loose") — "to let pass through".
commonMistakes: пропустить мимо ушей is a figurative idiom meaning "to let it go in one ear and out the other".

examples.gloss: Security let us through without a check.
The filter only lets clean water through.

synonymComparison.note: a more specific synonym for 'to miss' (an opportunity).

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll let that go in one ear and out the other (fixed phrase).

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you miss the party?

etymology: Derived from an archaic здравие.
commonMistakes: За ваше здоровье! is the standard toast, "To your health!"

etymology: Derived from выйти ("to exit").
commonMistakes: выход из ситуации is a figurative collocation meaning "a way out of a situation / a solution".

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of laughing; засмеяться is the perfective partner marking the onset of laughter.
etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to laugh".
commonMistakes: Takes смеяться над + instrumental (смеяться над собой = "to laugh at oneself").

examples.gloss: The whole room burst out laughing together.

synonymComparison.note: a synonym for 'to giggle,' a smaller/softer kind of laughter.

past.n.gloss: Everything seemed to laugh along with them.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We laugh at our own mistakes.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you laugh at this movie?

etymology: Borrowed from Italian banco ("a money-changer's table").
commonMistakes: берег ("shore") sounds somewhat similar but is unrelated — don't confuse it with банк.

etymology: An affectionate diminutive of дитя ("child").
commonMistakes: A very intimate term of address used for a lover or a child.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of getting off/down; use сходить (the same form) for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: Prefix с- ("down") plus идти ("to go").
commonMistakes: сойти с ума is a standard idiom meaning "to lose one's mind".

examples.ru: Она сошла с автобуса на остановке.
examples.gloss: She got off the bus at the stop.
The snow melted away in April.
Passengers get off at the next station.

examples.ru: Он сходит с ума от стресса.
examples.gloss: He's going crazy from stress (fixed phrase).

synonymComparison.note: сойти (specifically 'to get off/descend from a vehicle') is close to выйти ('to exit,' more general).

past.m.gloss: He dropped out of the race.

past.f.ru: Она сошла с ума от горя.
past.f.gloss: She went nearly mad with grief.

past.n.gloss: Everything went off without a hitch.

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I'll get off at the next stop.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll get off at this stop.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you get off at the last stop?

imperative.pl.gloss: Get off at the next stop.

etymology: The adverbial form of лёгкий ("light/easy").
commonMistakes: легко сказать is a standard idiom meaning "easy to say (but hard to do)".

etymology: Borrowed from French officier, ultimately from Latin officium ("duty").
commonMistakes: As an animate noun, its accusative equals its genitive (увидеть офицера).

etymology: Derived from an archaic ведать ("to know"); the original sense is "one who saw and knows".
commonMistakes: Distinguish свидетельство (a testimony/certificate, a noun) from свидетель (a witness, a person).

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "sacred".
commonMistakes: The nominalized use (святой = "a saint") is also common — distinguish it from the adjective use.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of reaching a destination; use добираться for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: Prefix до- ("to reach") plus an archaic брать (which once also carried a sense of "to advance").
commonMistakes: Как добраться? is the standard travel-phrase for "how do I get there?"

example.gloss: We made it to the hotel.

examples.gloss: She got to the bottom of the truth (figurative).
It takes me an hour to get to work.

synonymComparison.note: добраться ('to reach,' general, any means) differs from доехать ('to reach by vehicle,' more specific).

past.m.gloss: He made it to the summit.

past.pl.ru: Мы добрались до границы к утру.
past.pl.gloss: We reached the border by morning.

nonpast.1pl.ru: Мы доберёмся до места к вечеру.
nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll reach the place by evening.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you get there without issue?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll make it to the final.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of discovering; use обнаруживать for repeated/ongoing discovery.
etymology: Prefix об- plus наружу ("outward") — "to bring into the open".
commonMistakes: Distinguish найти (simply find) from обнаружить (discover unexpectedly, more literary in tone).

examples.gloss: She discovered the item was missing.
He's showing a talent for music.

synonymComparison.note: обнаружить ('to discover,' through investigation/chance) differs from найти ('to find,' more general).

past.n.gloss: Everything came to light by chance.

past.pl.gloss: We discovered a discrepancy in the data.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: He'll find the error in the code.

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We'll identify the cause of the failure.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Will you detect the violation?

imperative.sg.gloss: Find the source of the problem.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "small"; a quantity adverb.
commonMistakes: мало is followed by a genitive noun (мало времени = "little time").

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed impersonal event of "succeeding/working out"; use удаваться for repeated/ongoing instances.
etymology: Prefix у- plus an archaic дать ("to give") in reflexive form — "a result is given".
commonMistakes: Used as an impersonal verb with a dative experiencer (мне удалось = "I managed to").

example.gloss: I managed to finish the work.

examples.gloss: He always manages to find a solution.
I rarely manage to get enough sleep.

synonymComparison.note: удаться ('to succeed,' a stronger success nuance) differs from получиться ('to turn out,' more neutral).

past.f.gloss: The surgery went off without complications.

nonpast.1sg.ru: Удамся ли я этой роли — покажет время.
nonpast.1sg.gloss: (rare literary usage) Whether I'll succeed in this role, time will tell.

nonpast.2sg.ru: Удашься ли ты в этом деле, зависит от тебя.
nonpast.2sg.gloss: (rare literary usage) Whether you'll succeed in this matter depends on you.

nonpast.3sg.gloss: She'll manage to find a job.

nonpast.1pl.ru: Удадимся ли мы в этом плане — увидим.
nonpast.1pl.gloss: (rare literary usage) Whether we'll succeed in this plan, we'll see.

nonpast.2pl.ru: Удадитесь ли вы в новой роли, покажет опыт.
nonpast.2pl.gloss: (rare literary usage) Whether you'll succeed in the new role, experience will show.

nonpast.3pl.gloss: They'll manage to reach an agreement.

etymology: Derived from сделать ("to do/make"); the sense is "a deal/transaction".
commonMistakes: сделка с совестью is a figurative idiom meaning "a compromise against one's conscience".

aspectUsage: Imperfective for the ongoing act of thanking; use the perfective поблагодарить for a single completed expression of thanks.
etymology: благо ("good") plus дарить ("to give") — "to give a good thing → to thank".
commonMistakes: Takes благодарить за + accusative (благодарить за помощь).

example.gloss: I thank you for your help.

examples.gloss: He always thanks people for gifts.

synonymComparison.note: a related word of a different part of speech: благодарить is a verb ('to thank'), спасибо is the interjection 'thank you.'

past.m.gloss: He thanked the heavens for his luck.

past.f.gloss: She thanked them for their patience.

past.n.gloss: Everything seemed to silently thank fate (figurative).

nonpast.1sg.gloss: I thank you for your attention.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: Do you thank your parents for their support?

nonpast.1pl.gloss: We thank our clients for their trust.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: Do you thank your colleagues for their work?

imperative.pl.gloss: Be thankful for all the good things.

etymology: Derived from an archaic раз- ("to split"); the sense is "split apart → different".
commonMistakes: Its plural разные often has a generalizing sense, "various/all kinds of".

etymology: в plus место ("place") — "in place of".
commonMistakes: вместо requires the genitive (вместо меня, not "вместо мне").

etymology: Derived from ударить ("to strike").
commonMistakes: удар судьбы is a figurative idiom meaning "a blow of fate / a great misfortune".

etymology: на plus столько ("that much").
commonMistakes: Sometimes paired with насколько to express a comparison ("as much as").

aspectUsage: Perfective for the archaic, formal/honorific act of "gracing [a place] with one's presence". Its imperfective partner жаловать is now archaic, surviving mainly in the sense "to grant/bestow".
etymology: Prefix по- plus an archaic жаловать ("to grant/bestow").
commonMistakes: добро пожаловать is a fixed phrase meaning "welcome" — learn it as a unit, not literally.

examples.gloss: Please come to the table (archaic register).

synonymComparison.note: a more general/modern synonym for 'to welcome.' Пожаловать is almost exclusively used in добро пожаловать.

nonpast.1sg.ru: Пожалую к вам в гости на днях.
nonpast.1sg.gloss: (archaic) I shall pay you a visit one of these days.

nonpast.2sg.gloss: (archaic) Will you come visit us tomorrow?

nonpast.1pl.gloss: (archaic) We shall visit you with the whole family.

nonpast.2pl.gloss: (archaic) Will you come to our celebration?

nonpast.3pl.gloss: (archaic) The guests will arrive by evening.

imperative.sg.gloss: (archaic) Come this way, you'll be our guest.

imperative.pl.gloss: (archaic fixed phrase) Please come to the table.

aspectUsage: Perfective for a single completed act of raising/lifting; use поднимать for repeated/ongoing lifting.
etymology: Prefix под- plus an archaic нять ("to take") — "to take up from below".
